children.title: Cumulative Regret

knowledge_statements.title: Cumulative Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frequentist latent-function regret for sequential maximization with noisy observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a nonempty decision set, let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attain its maximum at \(x^\star\), and let \(x_t\) be the possibly history-dependent point evaluated at round \(t\). The instantaneous regret and cumulative regret through horizon \(T\in\mathbb N\) are
\[
r_t=f(x^\star)-f(x_t),\qquad R_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_t.
\]
These losses use latent objective values, even when the observations used to select \(x_t\) are noisy. If the algorithm or observations are random, expected cumulative regret is \(\mathbb E[R_T]\), with expectation over the stated sources of randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative regret sums, over all evaluations, the latent objective-value loss relative to a global maximizer; its expectation averages algorithmic and observation randomness.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) attains a finite maximum on \(\mathcal X\).
\(x_t\) is measurable with respect to the information available before round \(t\).

notation.meaning: A global maximizer of the latent objective.
Instantaneous latent-function regret at round t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic representation of cumulative regret and its implication for the best latent value among evaluated points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T[f(x^\star)-f(x_t)]\), \[R_T=T f(x^\star)-\sum_{t=1}^T f(x_t).\] If \(x_T^{\mathrm{best}}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{1\le t\le T}f(x_t)\), then \[0\le f(x^\star)-f(x_T^{\mathrm{best}})=\min_{1\le t\le T}r_t\le R_T/T.\] This oracle implication does not ensure that an implementable noisy-data recommendation selects \(x_T^{\mathrm{best}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative regret is optimal cumulative reward minus realized cumulative reward, and its average bounds the latent gap of the best evaluated point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) attains a finite maximum at \(x^\star\).

notation.meaning: An evaluated location with greatest latent objective value through T.

knowledge_statements.title: Reward Identity and Best-Evaluated-Point Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value opportunity loss accumulated across a finite sequence of evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f^*=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)$ and let $\phi_i=f(x_i)$ be the objective value at evaluation $i$. The instantaneous regret at evaluation $i$ is
\[
\rho_i=f^*-\phi_i.
\]
After $\tau$ evaluations, cumulative regret is
\[
R_\tau=\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\rho_i=\tau f^*-\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\phi_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Instantaneous regret is the gap between the global optimum value and the value obtained at one evaluation. Cumulative regret is the sum of those gaps over the evaluation horizon.
assumptions_latex: f^*=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)
\phi_i=f(x_i),\quad i=1,\ldots,\tau
\tau\in\mathbb N

children.title: Average Regret
children.top_down_role: Horizon-normalized online performance derived from cumulative regret.

knowledge_statements.title: Average Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Horizon-normalized cumulative regret for latent-objective maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For horizon \(T\ge 1\), suppose the cumulative regret is \(R_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(f(x^\star)-f(x_t)\bigr)\). The average regret is
\[
\overline R_T=\frac{R_T}{T}=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(f(x^\star)-f(x_t)\bigr).
\]
For a randomized policy or noisy observation process, expected average regret is \(\mathbb E[\overline R_T]=\mathbb E[R_T]/T\), provided \(R_T\) is integrable. Average regret measures opportunity loss per evaluation rather than total loss over the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average regret is cumulative latent-objective regret divided by the evaluation horizon, and therefore measures opportunity loss per evaluation.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\) and \(T\ge 1\).
\(R_T\) is integrable when expected average regret is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline R_T=R_T/T\), and \(\mathbb E[\overline R_T]=\mathbb E[R_T]/T\) when integrable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of best-observed simple regret with average cumulative regret, including failure of the converse implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f^*=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)$, $\phi_i=f(x_i)$, $r_\tau=f^*-\max_{1\le i\le\tau}\phi_i$, and $R_\tau=\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}(f^*-\phi_i)$. For every $\tau\ge1$,
\[
0\le r_\tau\le\frac{R_\tau}{\tau}.
\]
Consequently, the no-regret condition $R_\tau/\tau\to0$, equivalently $R_\tau=o(\tau)$, implies $r_\tau\to0$. The converse is false in general: a policy can attain progressively better best-observed values while continuing to evaluate a fixed suboptimal point on a positive fraction of iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple regret is bounded above by average cumulative regret. Therefore vanishing average regret, equivalently sublinear cumulative regret, implies vanishing simple regret. Vanishing simple regret does not imply no regret, because a policy may retain increasingly good observations while continuing to make suboptimal evaluations at a positive frequency.
assumptions_latex: f^*=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)
\phi_i=f(x_i),\quad i=1,\ldots,\tau
r_\tau=f^*-\max_{1\le i\le\tau}\phi_i
R_\tau=\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}(f^*-\phi_i)
\tau\ge1

children.title: No-Regret Behavior
children.top_down_role: Long-run regimes in which average performance loss vanishes.

knowledge_statements.title: No-Regret Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic no-regret condition for cumulative or expected cumulative loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequential maximization policy is pathwise no-regret when
\[
\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{R_T}{T}=0,
\]
on every sample path in the asserted event, or almost surely when the guarantee is probabilistic. It is no-regret in expectation when each \(R_T\) is integrable and
\[
\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb E[R_T]}{T}=0.
\]
Equivalently, the corresponding pathwise or expected average regret converges to zero. The mode of convergence must be stated and cannot be inferred solely from a sublinear bound holding in another mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A policy is no-regret when cumulative regret grows sublinearly, equivalently when average regret converges to zero, in the explicitly stated convergence mode.
assumptions_latex: \(R_T\) is the cumulative latent-objective regret.
\(R_T\) is integrable for the expectation formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T=o(T)\) is equivalent to \(\overline R_T\to0\) in the same asserted mode.

notation.meaning: A quantity whose ratio to T converges to zero.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexamples separating expected and almost-sure no-regret without suitable tail control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Neither expected nor almost-sure no-regret implies the other without additional hypotheses. For the first direction, let independent Bernoulli variables satisfy \(\mathbb P(B_t=1)=1/(t\log t)\) for \(t\ge2\), and set \(r_t=tB_t\). Then \(\mathbb E[R_T]/T\to0\), while \(B_t=1\) infinitely often almost surely and hence \(R_t/t\ge1\) infinitely often. Conversely, let \(\mathbb P(N=n)=c/n^2\), where \(c^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}\), and set \(r_N=N^2\) and \(r_t=0\) otherwise. Then \(R_T/T\to0\) almost surely, whereas \(\mathbb E[R_T]/T=c\) for every \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected and almost-sure no-regret do not imply one another when regret increments lack suitable tail or uniform-integrability control.
assumptions_latex: The examples allow nonnegative unbounded instantaneous regret.
All regret increments are defined on a common probability space.

notation.meaning: Rare Bernoulli event at round t.
Random round of a single large regret increment.

children.title: Horizon-Averaged Efficiency
children.top_down_role: Interpretation of average regret as sustained online efficiency.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Averaged Efficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of finite-horizon cumulative-regret bounds into per-evaluation guarantees without changing or conflating guarantee modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\overline R_T=R_T/T\) for \(T\ge1\), and let \(B(T)\ge0\). A deterministic or pathwise bound \(R_T\le B(T)\) implies \(\overline R_T\le B(T)/T\) on the same path or event. An expectation bound \(\mathbb E[R_T]\le B(T)\), with \(R_T\) integrable, implies \(\mathbb E[\overline R_T]\le B(T)/T\). A per-horizon probability bound \(\mathbb P(R_T\le B(T))\ge1-\delta_T\) implies \(\mathbb P(\overline R_T\le B(T)/T)\ge1-\delta_T\). If \(B(T)=o(T)\), the deterministic or common-event version yields \(\overline R_T\to0\) on that event; the per-horizon version yields convergence in probability when additionally \(\delta_T\to0\). In particular, for \(T\ge2\), \(B(T)\le C T^\alpha(\log T)^\beta\), where \(C>0\), \(0\le\alpha<1\), and \(\beta\ge0\), gives \(B(T)/T\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dividing a cumulative-regret bound by the positive horizon gives the corresponding average-regret bound in the same guarantee mode. A sublinear bound yields vanishing average regret pathwise on the event where it holds, in expectation for an expected bound, or in probability when the failure probabilities also vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\), \(T\ge1\), and \(B(T)\ge0\).
The cumulative-regret bound and its deterministic, expectation, or probability mode are explicitly stated.
\(R_T\) is integrable when an expectation bound is used.
For convergence in probability from per-horizon bounds, \(B(T)=o(T)\) and \(\delta_T\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In the corresponding mode, the horizon-normalized bound is \(B(T)/T\); sublinear \(B(T)\) gives the mode-specific vanishing conclusion stated above.

notation.meaning: A finite-horizon upper bound on cumulative regret in a declared guarantee mode.
Failure probability for the horizon-T probability bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Failure Probability Does Not Imply Vanishing Average Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that sublinear per-horizon bounds with nonvanishing failure probability do not yield convergence in probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\delta\in(0,1)\). For every \(T\ge1\), let \(Z_T\) be Bernoulli with \(P(Z_T=1)=\delta\), and set \(R_T=T Z_T\). Then \[P(R_T\le0)=1-\delta,\] so the per-horizon cumulative-regret bound \(B(T)=0=o(T)\) holds with confidence \(1-\delta\). Nevertheless \(\overline R_T=R_T/T=Z_T\), and therefore \[P(\overline R_T>1/2)=\delta\] for every \(T\). Thus \(\overline R_T\) does not converge to zero in probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sublinear per-horizon bound with a fixed nonzero failure probability need not make average regret vanish in probability.
assumptions_latex: The statements are separate per-horizon probability bounds, not one simultaneous event.

notation.meaning: Bernoulli indicator of the bad event at horizon T

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal latent-value loss of a recommendation after a finite noisy-evaluation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attain its maximum at \(x^\star\). After \(T\) noisy evaluations, let \(\widehat x_T\in\mathcal X\) be a recommendation measurable with respect to the resulting data and any algorithmic randomness. Its simple regret is
\[
r_T^{\mathrm s}=f(x^\star)-f(\widehat x_T).
\]
This definition evaluates the latent objective, not the noisy response observed at \(\widehat x_T\). Conditional or unconditional expected simple regret is obtained by taking the corresponding expectation of \(r_T^{\mathrm s}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple regret is the latent objective-value gap between a global maximizer and the terminal recommendation after the evaluation budget is exhausted.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) attains a finite maximum on \(\mathcal X\).
\(\widehat x_T\) is measurable with respect to terminal information.

notation.meaning: Simple regret of the terminal recommendation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Universal Simple-Regret Convergence Characterized by Dense Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes policies having simple-regret convergence for every continuous objective on a compact metric domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a compact metric space. An optimization policy converges in simple regret for every continuous function \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) if and only if its set of observed points \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}\{x_i\}\) is always dense in \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact metric space, a policy converges in simple regret for every continuous objective exactly when its observed points are always dense in the domain.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal X\text{ is a compact metric space}
f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\text{ ranges over continuous functions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall f\in C(\mathcal X),\ r_n(f)\to0\right]\iff\left[\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}\{x_i\}\text{ is always dense in }\mathcal X\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conversion from Cumulative Regret to Simple Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion obtained by recommending according to empirical action frequencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi=(\pi_t)_{t=1}^{n}\) be a policy and define \[\pi_{n+1}(i\mid a_1,x_1,\ldots,a_n,x_n)=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb I\{a_t=i\}.\] Then, on a bandit \(\nu\), \[R_n^{\mathrm{SIMPLE}}\bigl((\pi_t)_{t=1}^{n+1},\nu\bigr)=\frac{R_n(\pi,
u)}{n}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the terminal arm is sampled according to the empirical frequencies of the first n actions, its simple regret equals the original policy's cumulative regret divided by n.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi=(\pi_t)_{t=1}^{n}\) is a policy on bandit \(\nu\).
Conditioned on the observed history, the terminal policy assigns arm \(i\) probability \(n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb I\{a_t=i\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple regret based on latent objective values at evaluated locations, with the noisy-observation caveat and a distinct posterior-mean convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f^*=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)$ and let $\phi_i=f(x_i)$ for the $\tau$ evaluated locations. The best-observed-value simple regret is
\[
r_\tau=f^*-\max_{1\le i\le\tau}\phi_i.
\]
Thus $r_\tau\ge0$, and $r_\tau=0$ if and only if at least one evaluated location attains the global maximum. When evaluations are noisy, this latent-value criterion is interpreted under the tacit large-sample premise that the observations become sufficiently informative about the $\phi_i$. A distinct convention defines posterior-mean simple regret by $r_\tau^{\mu}=f^*-\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu_{\mathcal D_\tau}(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Best-observed-value simple regret is the global optimum value minus the best latent objective value attained at an evaluated location. It is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when a global maximizer has been evaluated. With noisy observations, its interpretation presumes that the data eventually reveal the latent values sufficiently well. A separate convention uses the maximum posterior mean instead.
assumptions_latex: f^*=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)
\phi_i=f(x_i),\quad i=1,\ldots,\tau
\text{For the noisy-data interpretation, observations are asymptotically sufficiently informative about the latent }\phi_i.

children.title: Bayes Simple Regret
children.top_down_role: Terminal optimization loss averaged under a prior model.

knowledge_statements.title: Bayes Simple Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prior-predictive terminal simple regret for Bayesian optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a random objective with prior distribution \(\Pi\), let \(X^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}F(x)\) be measurably selected, and let \(\widehat X_T\) be the recommendation produced from \(T\) noisy observations. The Bayes simple regret is
\[
\mathcal R_T^{\mathrm{Bayes}}=\mathbb E_{F\sim\Pi,\,Y,\,U}\!\left[F(X^\star)-F(\widehat X_T)\right],
\]
where the expectation includes the prior, observation noise \(Y\), and algorithmic randomness \(U\). Equivalently, it is the prior-predictive expectation of ordinary simple regret, provided the displayed gap is integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bayes simple regret averages terminal latent-value loss over the objective prior, observation noise, and any algorithmic randomization.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) almost surely attains a finite maximum on \(\mathcal X\).
\(X^\star\) and \(\widehat X_T\) are measurable selections.
\(F(X^\star)-F(\widehat X_T)\) is integrable.

notation.meaning: Prior distribution over latent objective functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posterior-Risk Representation of Bayes Simple Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tower-property representation and conditional Bayes action for terminal simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_T^\star=\mathbb E[\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}F(x)\mid\mathcal D_T]\) and \(\mu_T(x)=\mathbb E[F(x)\mid\mathcal D_T]\). For any \(\mathcal D_T\)-measurable recommendation \(\widehat X_T\), \[\mathcal R_T^{\mathrm{Bayes}}=\mathbb E\left[V_T^\star-\mu_T(\widehat X_T)\right].\] Consequently, over a declared measurable action set, a measurable posterior-mean maximizer minimizes conditional expected simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bayes simple regret is expected posterior opportunity loss, and posterior-mean maximization is its conditional Bayes action.
assumptions_latex: The optimal and recommended latent values are integrable.
\(\widehat X_T\) is measurable with respect to terminal data.
A measurable posterior-mean maximizer exists for the optimality conclusion.

notation.meaning: Posterior expectation of the latent optimal value.

children.title: Optimizer Identification
children.top_down_role: Terminal objectives centered on selecting an optimizer or optimizer region.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes identifying at least one latent optimizer from covering the complete optimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X^\star=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)
eq\varnothing\), and let \(C_T\subseteq\mathcal X\) be data-dependent. One-optimizer identification is the event \(C_T\cap X^\star
eq\varnothing\), whereas full-set identification is the event \(X^\star\subseteq C_T\). Thus \(\{X^\star\subseteq C_T\}\subseteq\{C_T\cap X^\star
eq\varnothing\}\). The inclusion can be strict when \(X^\star\) contains multiple points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Containing at least one optimizer and containing every optimizer are distinct criteria; full-set identification is stronger when optima are tied.
assumptions_latex: \(X^\star\neq\varnothing\).
\(C_T\) is a measurable random set under the declared probability semantics.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Optimizer and Full-Set Identification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posterior, Prior-Predictive, and Uniform Optimizer Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates three probability conventions for optimizer-set coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_T\) be data-dependent and let \(A_T=\{X^\star\cap C_T\ne\varnothing\}\). If under a joint prior-data model
\[\Pi(A_T\mid\mathcal D_T)\ge1-\delta\quad\text{almost surely},\]
then the tower property gives prior-predictive coverage \(\mathbb P_\Pi(A_T)\ge1-\delta\). This averaged statement does not imply the uniform sampling guarantee
\[\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}P_f(A_T)\ge1-\delta.\]
Such an implication requires an additional calibration or coverage theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior optimizer credibility yields prior-predictive coverage under the same joint model, but not uniform fixed-objective sampling coverage.
assumptions_latex: \(C_T\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal D_T\).
The posterior and prior-predictive probabilities arise from the same joint prior-data model.

notation.meaning: event that the reported set contains at least one optimizer
posterior probability conditional on the observed data
sampling law with latent objective f fixed

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior, Prior-Predictive, and Uniform Optimizer Coverage

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a full optimizer-covering set from a simultaneous objective band.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L_T,U_T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), and suppose that on an event \(E_T\), \(L_T(x)\le f(x)\le U_T(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\). Define
\[C_T=\left\{x\in\mathcal X:U_T(x)\ge \sup_{z\in\mathcal X}L_T(z)\right\}.\]
Then on \(E_T\), every global maximizer belongs to \(C_T\). Consequently, if \(P_f(E_T)\ge1-\delta\), then \(P_f(X^\star\subseteq C_T)\ge1-\delta\), and therefore \(P_f(X^\star\cap C_T\ne\varnothing)\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simultaneous objective band yields an optimizer confidence set by retaining points whose upper bound reaches the largest lower bound; on the band event it contains every maximizer.
assumptions_latex: \(X^\star=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
The band holds simultaneously over \(\mathcal X\) on \(E_T\).
\(C_T\) is measurable under the declared probability semantics.
knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous-Band Optimizer-Set Certificate
Optimizer Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-confidence certification of membership in the latent optimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X^\star=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), let \(\mathcal D_T\) be the data after \(T\) noisy evaluations, and let \(C_T=C_T(\mathcal D_T)\subseteq\mathcal X\) be a reported set. At confidence level \(1-\delta\), \(C_T\) is an optimizer-identification certificate if
\[
\mathbb P_f\!\left(X^\star\cap C_T\ne\varnothing\right)\ge1-\delta.
\]
If a singleton \(C_T=\{\widehat x_T\}\) is reported, the condition becomes \(\mathbb P_f(\widehat x_T\in X^\star)\ge1-\delta\). The probability must specify whether coverage is frequentist, prior-predictive, or posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimizer-identification certificate reports a set that contains at least one true latent maximizer with the stated confidence and probability semantics.
assumptions_latex: \(X^\star\) is nonempty.
\(C_T\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal D_T\).

notation.meaning: Set of global maximizers of the latent objective.

children.title: Value-Tolerance Certification
children.top_down_role: Certificates based on acceptable terminal objective-value error.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a simultaneous latent-objective band into a value-tolerance certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(L_T,U_T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(L_T(x)\le f(x)\le U_T(x)\) simultaneously for every \(x\in\mathcal X\) on an event \(E_T\). For a recommendation \(\widehat x_T\), define \(B_T=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}U_T(x)-L_T(\widehat x_T)\). On \(E_T\), \(f^\star-f(\widehat x_T)\le B_T\). Consequently, if \(\mathbb P_f(E_T)\ge1-\delta\) and \(B_T\le\varepsilon\) almost surely, then \(\mathbb P_f(f^\star-f(\widehat x_T)\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\). More generally, on issuance only the event inclusion \(E_T\cap\{B_T\le\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{f^\star-f(\widehat x_T)\le\varepsilon\}\) is automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simultaneous objective band bounds simple regret by the largest upper bound minus the recommendation's lower bound; an unconditional confidence claim also requires the threshold condition with the corresponding probability.
assumptions_latex: \(L_T(x)\le f(x)\le U_T(x)\) simultaneously for all \(x\) on \(E_T\).
\(\mathbb P_f(E_T)\ge1-\delta\).
\(\sup_x U_T(x)<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Event on which the objective band is simultaneously valid.
Band-derived upper bound on terminal simple regret.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Band Value-Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Bands Do Not Supply Simultaneous Value Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a global value-gap certificate when only marginal pointwise coverage is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Pointwise statements \(\mathbb P_f(L_T(x)\le f(x)\le U_T(x))\ge1-\delta\) for every fixed \(x\) do not imply \(\mathbb P_f(\forall x,\ L_T(x)\le f(x)\le U_T(x))\ge1-\delta\). For example, on a two-point domain, disjoint band-failure events of probability \(\delta\) at the two points give marginal coverage \(1-\delta\) but simultaneous coverage \(1-2\delta\). Therefore the uniform-band value-gap certificate cannot be justified from marginal bands alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginal confidence bands at individual decisions do not provide the simultaneous coverage needed for a global value-gap certificate.
assumptions_latex: The domain contains at least two distinct points.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Bands Do Not Supply Simultaneous Value Certification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-membership formulation of terminal value tolerance for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f^\star=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)<\infty\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define \(X_\varepsilon^\star=\{x\in\mathcal X:f^\star-f(x)\le\varepsilon\}\). Then \(f^\star-f(\widehat x_T)\le\varepsilon\) if and only if \(\widehat x_T\in X_\varepsilon^\star\). Hence any probability guarantee for the value gap is equivalently a probability guarantee for membership in \(X_\varepsilon^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon value-gap guarantee is exactly membership of the recommendation in the epsilon-optimal set.
assumptions_latex: \(f^\star<\infty\).
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Optimal Set Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posterior, Prior-Predictive, and Uniform Value-Tolerance Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates three probability conventions for near-optimal-value certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_T=\{f^\star-f(\widehat x_T)\le\varepsilon\}\). If under a joint prior-data model
\[\Pi(A_T\mid\mathcal D_T)\ge1-\delta\quad\text{almost surely},\]
then the tower property gives \(\mathbb P_\Pi(A_T)\ge1-\delta\). This prior-predictive guarantee does not generally imply
\[\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}P_f(A_T)\ge1-\delta.\]
Uniform sampling validity requires an additional calibration or coverage theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior near-optimality credibility yields prior-predictive coverage under the same model, but not uniform fixed-objective sampling validity.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat x_T\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal D_T\).
The posterior and prior-predictive probabilities arise from the same joint prior-data model.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(0<\delta<1\).

Value-Tolerance Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-confidence certification that a recommendation is near-optimal in latent value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f^\star=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), and let \(\widehat x_T\) be a recommendation based on data \(\mathcal D_T\). For tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and error level \(\delta\in(0,1)\), the report \((\widehat x_T,\varepsilon,\delta)\) is a value-tolerance certificate when its stated probability semantics ensure
\[
\mathbb P_f\!\left(f^\star-f(\widehat x_T)\le\varepsilon\right)\ge1-\delta.
\]
A posterior certificate replaces this sampling statement by \(\mathbb P(f^\star-f(\widehat x_T)\le\varepsilon\mid\mathcal D_T)\ge1-\delta\); the two interpretations must not be conflated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-tolerance certificate guarantees, with stated confidence semantics, that the recommendation's latent value lies within epsilon of the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f^\star\) is finite.
\(\widehat x_T\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal D_T\).
\(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(0<\delta<1\).

children.title: Indifference-Zone Criteria
children.top_down_role: Selection criteria incorporating practically negligible performance differences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform probability-of-correct-selection requirement over finite-alternative instances having a declared minimum best-versus-second-best gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite alternatives \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\) with means \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\), let \(i^\star\) be the unique best alternative and let \(\Delta>0\). The indifference-zone parameter class is \[\Theta_\Delta=\left\{\mu:\mu_{i^\star}-\max_{j\ne i^\star}\mu_j\ge\Delta\right\}.\] A selection procedure \(\widehat i\) provides a \((\Delta,1-\alpha)\) indifference-zone guarantee when \[\inf_{\mu\in\Theta_\Delta}\mathbb P_\mu(\widehat i=i^\star)\ge1-\alpha.\] The strict or non-strict gap boundary must be declared. Instances with ties or gaps below \(\Delta\) are outside this classical guarantee; selecting any alternative within a value tolerance is instead a probability-of-good-selection criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical indifference-zone criterion uniformly guarantees correct selection when a unique best finite alternative exceeds every competitor by at least the declared gap.
assumptions_latex: The alternative set is finite.
Every instance in \(\Theta_\Delta\) has a unique best alternative.
\(\Delta>0\) and \(0<\alpha<1\).
The sampling distribution and probability measure \(\mathbb P_\mu\) are specified.

notation.meaning: Minimum best-versus-second-best mean gap defining the indifference zone.
Parameter class satisfying the declared separation condition.
Maximum allowed probability of incorrect selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Indifference-Zone Correct-Selection Criterion
Indifference-Zone Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection criterion when alternatives within a prescribed value gap are operationally equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f^\star=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\) and fix an indifference-zone width \(\Delta>0\). The acceptable set is
\[
X_\Delta=\{x\in\mathcal X:f^\star-f(x)\le\Delta\}.
\]
A terminal selection rule satisfies the \((\Delta,\delta)\) indifference-zone criterion if
\[
\mathbb P_f(\widehat x_T\in X_\Delta)\ge1-\delta.
\]
For finite alternatives, a stronger correct-selection formulation may instead require identifying the unique maximizer whenever its value exceeds every competitor by at least \(\Delta\). The chosen formulation and boundary convention must be declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indifference-zone criterion accepts recommendations within a prescribed latent-value gap and requires the acceptable-set selection probability to exceed the stated confidence.
assumptions_latex: \(f^\star\) is finite.
\(\Delta>0\) and \(0<\delta<1\).
\(\widehat x_T\) is a measurable terminal recommendation.

notation.meaning: Set of alternatives within Delta of optimal value.
Allowed probability of selecting outside the acceptable set.

children.title: Evaluated-Point Recommendations
children.top_down_role: Recommendations restricted to previously evaluated locations.

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluated-Point Recommendations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal recommendations constrained to the set of sampled locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given evaluation locations \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathcal X\), define the evaluated set \(E_T=\{x_t:1\le t\le T\}\). An evaluated-point recommendation is a terminal decision \(\widehat x_T\) satisfying
\[
\widehat x_T\in E_T.
\]
Under noisy observations \(y_t=f(x_t)+\varepsilon_t\), membership in \(E_T\) does not prescribe how \(\widehat x_T\) is selected: it may maximize a denoised estimate, posterior mean, empirical replication mean, or validation statistic over \(E_T\). Its simple regret is still computed from the latent value \(f(\widehat x_T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluated-point recommendation must be one of the locations sampled by the algorithm, although its selection score may use noise-aware estimation.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t\in\mathcal X\) for every \(1\le t\le T\).

notation.meaning: Set of locations evaluated through time T.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of sampling loss from noisy selection loss among evaluated locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_T^{\mathrm{best}}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in E_T}f(x)\) and \(\widehat x_T\in E_T\). Then \[f(x^\star)-f(\widehat x_T)=\bigl[f(x^\star)-f(x_T^{\mathrm{best}})\bigr]+\bigl[f(x_T^{\mathrm{best}})-f(\widehat x_T)\bigr],\] where both terms are nonnegative. Thus evaluated-point simple regret vanishes exactly when both sampling loss and selection loss vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluated-point simple regret splits into failure to sample a good point and failure to select the best sampled point.
assumptions_latex: \(E_T\ne\varnothing\).
\(\widehat x_T\in E_T\).

children.title: Posterior-Surface Recommendations
children.top_down_role: Recommendations selected from a latent posterior summary over the full domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-domain recommendation obtained by optimizing a declared posterior latent-function summary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given terminal data \(\mathcal D_T\), let \(S_T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be a declared measurable posterior summary of the latent objective. A posterior-surface recommendation is a measurable selection \[\widehat x_T\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}S_T(x).\] It need not have been evaluated. The summary, recommendation domain, tie rule, and any approximation or nonattainment convention must be declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posterior-surface recommendation maximizes a declared latent posterior summary over its full recommendation domain and may be unevaluated.
assumptions_latex: \(S_T\) is measurable and determined by \(\mathcal D_T\).
An exact measurable maximizer exists, or an explicit approximate-maximization convention is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Posterior-Surface Recommendation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posterior-Mean Recommendation Is the Conditional Bayes Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayes-optimal posterior-surface choice under latent simple-regret loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_T(x)=\mathbb E[F(x)\mid\mathcal D_T]\) and suppose the relevant conditional expectations are finite. For every \(\mathcal D_T\)-measurable action \(a\), \[\mathbb E[\sup_xF(x)-F(a)\mid\mathcal D_T]=\mathbb E[\sup_xF(x)\mid\mathcal D_T]-\mu_T(a).\] Hence a measurable maximizer of \(\mu_T\) over the declared recommendation domain minimizes conditional expected simple regret. Other posterior summaries require a different declared loss or justification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under simple-regret loss, posterior-mean maximization is the conditional Bayes recommendation; arbitrary posterior summaries are not interchangeable with it.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional expectations are finite.
A posterior-mean maximizer admits a measurable selection.
knowledge_statements.title: Posterior-Mean Recommendation Is the Conditional Bayes Rule
Posterior-Surface Recommendations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-domain recommendation obtained by optimizing a posterior latent-function summary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Pi_T\) be the posterior distribution of the latent objective \(F\) given data \(\mathcal D_T\), and let \(S_T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be a specified posterior summary, such as \(S_T(x)=\mathbb E[F(x)\mid\mathcal D_T]\). A posterior-surface recommendation is any measurable selection
\[
\widehat x_T\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}S_T(x).
\]
The optimization ranges over the full domain, so \(\widehat x_T\) need not have been evaluated. The summary \(S_T\), tie-breaking rule, and existence or approximation convention for the maximizer must be stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posterior-surface recommendation maximizes a declared posterior summary over the full domain and may therefore be an unevaluated location.
assumptions_latex: \(S_T\) is measurable and determined by \(\mathcal D_T\).
\(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}S_T(x)\) admits a measurable selection.

children.title: Validated Recommendations
children.top_down_role: Recommendations assessed using confirmation evaluations or independent validation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional concentration for independently replicated assessment of a selected candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widetilde x_T\) be selected from \(\mathcal D_T\). Conditional on \(\mathcal D_T\), obtain independent responses \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\) at \(\widetilde x_T\) with conditional mean \(f(\widetilde x_T)\) and conditionally \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian centered noise. Then \[\mathbb E[\bar Z_m\mid\mathcal D_T]=f(\widetilde x_T),\qquad \mathbb P\left(|\bar Z_m-f(\widetilde x_T)|>\epsilon\mid\mathcal D_T\right)\le2\exp\left(-\frac{m\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\] The same statement need not hold when adaptively selected observations are reused without selection adjustment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fresh independent sub-Gaussian replications give an unbiased, exponentially concentrating assessment of an adaptively selected candidate.
assumptions_latex: Validation responses are conditionally independent of selection data given the selected candidate.
Validation noise is conditionally mean-zero and \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[\bar Z_m\mid\mathcal D_T]=f(\widetilde x_T),\quad \mathbb P(|\bar Z_m-f(\widetilde x_T)|>\epsilon\mid\mathcal D_T)\le2e^{-m\epsilon^2/(2\sigma^2)}.
knowledge_statements.title: Fresh-Replication Validation Guarantee
Validated Recommendations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recommendation semantics requiring data independent of the selection data for final assessment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widetilde x_T\) be a candidate selected from optimization data \(\mathcal D_T\), and let \(V_T\) be confirmation data generated conditionally independently of \(\mathcal D_T\) given the latent objective and \(\widetilde x_T\). A validated recommendation is a reported point \(\widehat x_T\) whose acceptance is determined by a prespecified measurable rule
\[
A_T(\widetilde x_T,V_T)\in\{0,1\},\qquad A_T(\widetilde x_T,V_T)=1,
\]
with \(\widehat x_T=\widetilde x_T\). The rule must declare the validation sample, statistic, threshold, and failure output. Reusing selection data alone does not constitute independent validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validated recommendation is accepted by a prespecified rule using confirmation data independent of the data that selected the candidate.
assumptions_latex: \(\widetilde x_T\) is measurable with respect to selection data \(\mathcal D_T\).
\(V_T\) is conditionally independent of \(\mathcal D_T\) given the latent objective and candidate.
\(A_T\) is prespecified and measurable.

notation.meaning: Candidate produced by the optimization stage.

children.title: Bayesian Average-Case Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Performance averaged under the assumed prior law.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage limit of prior-predictive guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An expectation under \(F\sim\Pi\) is unaffected by changing loss on a \(\Pi\)-null measurable set. Therefore \(\mathbb E_\Pi R_T(F)\le b_T\) does not, without extra assumptions, bound every fixed \(R_T(f)\) or transfer to a different objective-noise law \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average-case performance may ignore prior-null objectives and does not automatically transfer under model misspecification.
assumptions_latex: The guarantee averages only under the declared prior-predictive law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_\Pi R_T(F)\le b_T\not\Rightarrow R_T(f)\le b_T\ \forall f\).
knowledge_statements.title: Prior-Null and Misspecification Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic implication of a nonnegative prior-average risk bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_T(f)=\mathbb E[L_T\mid F=f]\ge0\). If \(\int R_T(f)\,\Pi(df)\le b_T\), then for every \(\eta>0\), \[\Pi\{f:R_T(f)>\eta\}\le b_T/\eta.\] This controls prior mass, not every fixed objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayes-risk bound limits the prior mass of objectives having large conditional risk but does not give a uniform fixed-function bound.
assumptions_latex: \(L_T\ge0\) is measurable and integrable.
A measurable version of the conditional risk is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Prior-Mass Consequence of Bayes Risk

assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\).
\(F\sim\Pi\), and \(L_T(F,\varepsilon,U)\) is nonnegative, measurable, and integrable under the joint law of \((F,\varepsilon,U)\).

notation.meaning: assumed probability law on objective functions
nonnegative performance loss through horizon T

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard prior-predictive definition of a Bayesian average-case performance guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prior-predictive performance semantics for noisy Bayesian optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\in\mathbb N\), let \(F\sim\Pi\) be a random objective, let \(Y_t=F(X_t)+\varepsilon_t\) for \(1\le t\le T\), and let \(U\) denote policy randomization. For a nonnegative integrable loss \(L_T(F,\varepsilon,U)\) and deterministic bound \(b_T\in[0,\infty)\), a Bayesian average-case guarantee is
\[\mathbb E_{F\sim\Pi,\,\varepsilon,\,U}\!\left[L_T(F,\varepsilon,U)\right]\le b_T.\]
The expectation uses the specified joint law of the objective, observation noise, and policy randomization; it does not assert the bound for every fixed objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayesian average-case guarantee bounds expected loss under the specified joint law of the objective prior, observation noise, and policy randomness, rather than uniformly over fixed objectives.
knowledge_statements.title: Bayesian Average-Case Guarantees

children.title: Frequentist Function-Class Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Performance for fixed objectives belonging to a prescribed regularity class.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimax Risk Representation of a Frequentist Function-Class Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-comparison representation for fixed-objective class-uniform expected performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function class \(\mathcal F\), algorithm family \(\mathfrak A\), and nonnegative measurable loss \(L_T(A,f,\varepsilon,U)\), define \[\mathcal R_T(A;\mathcal F)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,U}L_T(A,f,\varepsilon,U),\qquad \mathcal R_T^*(\mathcal F)=\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A}\mathcal R_T(A;\mathcal F).\] The supremum ranges over fixed deterministic objectives; the expectation does not average over a prior on \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Class-uniform frequentist expected performance is worst fixed-objective risk, and minimizing it over algorithms gives the minimax benchmark.
assumptions_latex: \(L_T\ge0\) is measurable for every \(A\in\mathfrak A\) and \(f\in\mathcal F\).
Each \(f\) is deterministic and fixed while feedback and algorithmic randomness are averaged.

notation.meaning: minimax frequentist risk over the function class

knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Risk Representation of a Frequentist Function-Class Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Bounds Need Not Yield a Uniform Class Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier-separation example for fixed-objective guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F=\{f_m:m\in\mathbb N\}\) and let a deterministic nonnegative loss satisfy \(L_T(f_m)=m\). For every fixed \(f_m\), the finite pointwise bound \(L_T(f_m)\le m\) holds, but \[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}L_T(f)=\infty.\] Thus finite objective-dependent bounds do not imply a single finite class-uniform bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-dependent pointwise bounds can all be finite while their worst-case bound over the function class is infinite.
assumptions_latex: The class contains the sequence \((f_m)_{m\in\mathbb N}\).
The loss is the displayed deterministic function of the fixed objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall f\in\mathcal F\ \exists b_f<\infty:L_T(f)\le b_f)\not\Rightarrow(\exists b<\infty\ \forall f\in\mathcal F:L_T(f)\le b).
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Bounds Need Not Yield a Uniform Class Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering of class-uniform frequentist risks as the fixed-objective class grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2\), then for every algorithm \(A\), \[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_1}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,U}L_T(A,f,\varepsilon,U)\le \sup_{f\in\mathcal F_2}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,U}L_T(A,f,\varepsilon,U).\] Consequently, for a fixed admissible algorithm family, \(\mathcal R_T^*(\mathcal F_1)\le\mathcal R_T^*(\mathcal F_2)\). The analogous ordering holds for worst-case exceedance probabilities at a fixed threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlarging the deterministic objective class cannot improve a class-uniform frequentist risk or its minimax value.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2\).
The same loss, feedback model, and admissible algorithm family are used for both classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2\Longrightarrow\mathcal R_T^*(\mathcal F_1)\le\mathcal R_T^*(\mathcal F_2).

notation.meaning: Minimax frequentist expected risk over function class F.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity under Function-Class Inclusion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical quantifier forms for frequentist performance over a deterministic function class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of deterministic objectives and let \(L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)\ge0\) be measurable. For fixed \(f\), a pointwise expectation guarantee is \(\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,U}L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)\le b_T(f)\); a class-uniform expectation guarantee is \[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,U}L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)\le b_T.\] Likewise, a class-uniform high-probability guarantee is \[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb P_{\varepsilon,U}\!\left(L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)>b_T(\delta)\right)\le\delta.\] In all forms the objective is fixed rather than averaged under a prior. Uniformity requires one deterministic bound for the whole class; it does not require one common success event over all \(f\) unless that stronger simultaneous statement is explicitly quantified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Frequentist function-class guarantees hold for fixed deterministic objectives and average only feedback and policy randomness; pointwise bounds may depend on the objective, whereas class-uniform bounds use one worst-class bound.
assumptions_latex: \(L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)\) is nonnegative and measurable for every \(f\in\mathcal F\).
Expectations exist as extended nonnegative expectations; a finite guarantee requires a finite bound.
\(\delta\in(0,1)\) for the probability form.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise and Class-Uniform Fixed-Objective Guarantees

assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and \(\mathcal F\) is a specified class of deterministic objectives.
For every \(f\in\mathcal F\), \(L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)\) is nonnegative and measurable under the joint law of \((\varepsilon,U)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,U}[L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)]\le b_T\) or \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb P_{\varepsilon,U}(L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)>b_T(\delta))\le\delta\), according to the stated guarantee mode.

notation.meaning: prescribed class of fixed objective functions
nonnegative performance loss through horizon T

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard frequentist distinction between fixed objectives and sampling or procedural randomness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform or pointwise guarantees for fixed objectives under repeated noise and algorithm randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\in\mathbb N\), let \(\mathcal F\) be a prescribed class of deterministic objectives, and let \(L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)\ge0\) be measurable for each \(f\in\mathcal F\). A class-uniform frequentist expectation guarantee with deterministic bound \(b_T\ge0\) is
\[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,U}\!\left[L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)\right]\le b_T.\]
For \(\delta\in(0,1)\), a class-uniform high-probability guarantee is
\[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb P_{\varepsilon,U}\!\left(L_T(f,\varepsilon,U)>b_T(\delta)\right)\le\delta.\]
Here each \(f\) is fixed. A pointwise guarantee instead quantifies a fixed \(f\in\mathcal F\) and may use a bound depending on that \(f\); it is weaker than class-uniform control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frequentist function-class guarantee treats the objective as fixed and controls performance over noise and policy randomness. A class-uniform guarantee uses one bound for every objective in the class, whereas a pointwise guarantee concerns a specified fixed objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Frequentist Function-Class Guarantees

children.title: Expectation Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Performance guarantees expressed through averaging over relevant randomness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Expectation Control Implies Marginal Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between history-conditional and unconditional mean-performance guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_T\ge0\) be integrable, let \(\mathcal G\) be a sub-\(\sigma\)-field, and let \(b_T\ge0\) be deterministic. If \(\mathbb E[L_T\mid\mathcal G]\le b_T\) almost surely, then \(\mathbb E[L_T]\le b_T\). The converse need not hold: an unconditional bound can average over histories whose conditional means lie above and below \(b_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional mean bound holding almost surely implies the corresponding unconditional expectation guarantee, but an unconditional bound need not hold after every history.
assumptions_latex: \(L_T\ge0\) is integrable.
\(\mathcal G\) is a sub-\(\sigma\)-field.
\(b_T\ge0\) is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Expectation Control Implies Marginal Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical mean-performance statement under an explicitly declared probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the declared law of all randomness being averaged and let \(L_T\ge0\) be measurable. A finite expectation guarantee at horizon \(T\) is \[\mathbb E_P[L_T]\le b_T<\infty.\] The law must state whether the objective is fixed and only feedback and policy randomization are averaged, or whether the objective is also prior-random. For a signed loss, integrability \(\mathbb E_P|L_T|<\infty\) is required. The inequality alone supplies no specified per-run failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation guarantee bounds mean loss under a fully specified probability law; signed losses require integrability, and mean control alone is not a confidence statement for individual runs.
assumptions_latex: \(L_T\) is measurable under \(P\).
For a finite nonnegative-loss guarantee, \(\mathbb E_P L_T<\infty\); a signed loss is integrable.
\(b_T\) is deterministic and finite.

notation.meaning: declared law of all averaged randomness

knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Loss Guarantee

assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\).
\(L_T\) is nonnegative, measurable, and integrable under \(P\).

notation.meaning: probability law defining all averaged randomness
deterministic upper bound on expected loss

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard mathematical form of an expected-loss guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-performance semantics for a nonnegative Bayesian-optimization loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\in\mathbb N\), let \(P\) be a specified probability law, let \(L_T\ge0\) be integrable under \(P\), and let \(b_T\in[0,\infty)\) be deterministic. An expectation guarantee at horizon \(T\) is
\[\mathbb E_P[L_T]\le b_T.\]
The law \(P\) must identify all averaged randomness. It may condition on a fixed objective and average only observation noise and policy randomization, or it may also average over a prior on the objective. This inequality alone specifies no confidence level for individual runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation guarantee bounds mean loss under an explicitly specified probability law, which must state whether the objective is fixed or prior-random; it does not by itself give a per-run confidence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Guarantees

children.title: High-Probability Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Performance guarantees qualified by an explicit failure probability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure-probability accounting for finitely many performance events under one probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\) be measurable events under \(P\), with \(P(E_i)\ge 1-\delta_i\) and \(\delta_i\ge0\). Then
\[P\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m E_i\right)\ge 1-\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_i.\]
Thus finitely many loss bounds hold simultaneously with failure probability at most the sum of their individual failure probabilities; independence is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite high-probability guarantees compose by adding their failure probabilities, without an independence assumption.
assumptions_latex: \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\) are measurable under the same probability law \(P\).
\(P(E_i^c)\le\delta_i\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: allocated failure probability for event i

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Composition of High-Probability Guarantees

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical success-event and failure-event forms with explicit objective and horizon quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the declared probability law, let \(L_T\) be measurable, and let \(\delta\in(0,1)\). A high-probability guarantee at horizon \(T\) is \[P(L_T\le b_T(\delta))\ge1-\delta,\] equivalently \(P(L_T>b_T(\delta))\le\delta\). Separate statements for each \(T\) may use different success events; a time-uniform guarantee instead requires one event \(E\) with \(P(E)\ge1-\delta\) on which every declared horizon bound holds. Likewise, \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}P_f(L_T>b_T(\delta))\le\delta\) is class-uniform in probability but does not assert a common event over all \(f\); that stronger claim requires an explicit simultaneous quantifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-probability guarantee bounds loss outside an event of probability at most delta; time-uniform and objective-simultaneous claims require stronger, explicit common-event quantifiers.
assumptions_latex: \(L_T\) is measurable under the declared law \(P\).
\(\delta\in(0,1)\), and \(b_T(\delta)\) is deterministic.
Uniform claims explicitly declare their objective and horizon quantifiers.

notation.meaning: common success event for a simultaneous claim

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence-Indexed Loss Guarantee

assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and \(b_T(\delta)\in\mathbb R\).
\(L_T\) is real-valued and measurable under \(P\).

notation.meaning: specified probability law governing the claim

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a high-probability performance bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Confidence-indexed performance semantics under an explicitly specified law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\in\mathbb N\), let \(P\) be a specified probability law, let \(L_T\) be a real-valued measurable loss, and let \(\delta\in(0,1)\). For a deterministic bound \(b_T(\delta)\in\mathbb R\), a high-probability guarantee is
\[P\!\left(L_T\le b_T(\delta)\right)\ge1-\delta,\]
equivalently \(P(L_T>b_T(\delta))\le\delta\). Whether the claim is pointwise or simultaneous over horizons, and pointwise or uniform over objectives, must be stated through additional quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a specified probability law, loss is at most a confidence-dependent bound except on an event of probability at most delta. Separate quantifiers determine whether the claim is simultaneous over horizons or uniform over objectives.
knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Guarantees

children.title: Tail-Risk Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Structural comparison between average performance control and rare-event protection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quantile Control Does Not Bound Exceptional-Tail Severity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point loss family separating a high-probability threshold from expectation and conditional tail magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and \(M>0\), and let \(L_M\) satisfy \[P(L_M=0)=1-\delta,\qquad P(L_M=M)=\delta.\] Then \[P(L_M\le0)=1-\delta,\qquad \operatorname{VaR}_{1-\delta}(L_M)=0,\] while \[\mathbb E[L_M]=\delta M,\qquad \operatorname{CVaR}_{1-\delta}(L_M)=M.\] Hence the fixed quantile bound permits arbitrarily large mean loss and upper-tail average as \(M\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loss that is zero with probability one minus delta and equals M otherwise has zero confidence quantile but tail average M.
assumptions_latex: CVaR uses the upper-tail Rockafellar–Uryasev convention at confidence level \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quantile Control Does Not Bound Exceptional-Tail Severity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Markov Conversion from Mean Loss to Tail Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distribution-free conversion of a nonnegative expectation bound into a confidence bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\ge0\) be integrable and suppose \(\mathbb E[L]\le b\). For every \(\delta\in(0,1)\),
\[P\!\left(L\le \frac{b}{\delta}\right)\ge1-\delta,\]
so \(\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\delta}(L)\le b/\delta\). The inverse-\(\delta\) dependence cannot be uniformly improved using only nonnegativity and the mean bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Markov's inequality converts a nonnegative mean-loss bound into a confidence bound with sharp inverse dependence on the failure probability.
assumptions_latex: \(L\ge0\) almost surely.
\(\mathbb E[L]\le b<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Markov Conversion from Mean Loss to Tail Control

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper-Tail CVaR Dominates the Corresponding VaR
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering between the tail-risk summaries used to interpret probabilistic loss guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) be an integrable real-valued loss and let \(0<\delta<1\). Under the upper-tail conventions
\[\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\delta}(L)=\inf\{z:P(L\le z)\ge1-\delta\},\qquad \operatorname{CVaR}_{1-\delta}(L)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R}\left\{z+\delta^{-1}\mathbb E[(L-z)_+]\right\},\]
one has
\[\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\delta}(L)\le \operatorname{CVaR}_{1-\delta}(L).\]
Thus an upper bound on this CVaR also bounds the corresponding VaR, whereas a VaR bound alone need not bound CVaR.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper-tail CVaR is at least the corresponding VaR, so CVaR control implies quantile control but not conversely.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is integrable.
VaR and CVaR use the displayed upper-loss-tail conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Tail CVaR Dominates the Corresponding VaR

assumptions_latex: \(L_T\) is real-valued and measurable under \(P\); integrability is additionally required for \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{1-\delta}(L_T)\).

notation.meaning: specified probability law of the loss
distribution function of the loss at horizon T
upper loss quantile at confidence level one minus delta

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard quantile and Rockafellar-Uryasev expected-shortfall representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile and expected-shortfall readings of high-probability loss bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a probability law, let \(L_T\) be a real-valued measurable loss with distribution function \(F_T(z)=P(L_T\le z)\), and let \(\delta\in(0,1)\). Define
\[\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\delta}(L_T)=\inf\{z\in\mathbb R:F_T(z)\ge1-\delta\}.\]
For any deterministic \(b_T(\delta)\in\mathbb R\),
\[P(L_T\le b_T(\delta))\ge1-\delta\quad\Rightarrow\quad\operatorname{VaR}_{1-\delta}(L_T)\le b_T(\delta).\]
If \(L_T\) is integrable, define
\[\operatorname{CVaR}_{1-\delta}(L_T)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R}\left\{z+\delta^{-1}\mathbb E_P[(L_T-z)_+]\right\}.\]
The quantile bound alone need not bound this upper-tail average because losses on the exceptional event can be arbitrarily large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-probability loss bound controls the corresponding loss quantile under a specified probability law, but it does not by itself control the average magnitude of losses in the exceptional tail.
knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Risk Interpretation

children.title: Finite-Time Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Performance control at specified finite evaluation horizons.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\subseteq\mathbb N\) is explicitly specified.
\(L_T\) is measurable under \(P\) for every \(T\in\mathcal T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(T\in\mathcal T\), the stated finite-horizon performance predicate holds; a time-uniform claim additionally controls all stated horizons on one event.

notation.meaning: specified probability law governing random performance

review_flags: locator supports finite-horizon terminology provisionally, but not yet the complete guarantee-quantifier distinction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonasymptotic performance control at explicitly quantified evaluation horizons.

source_refs.source_title: Approximate Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal T\subseteq\mathbb N\) be a specified set of finite horizons, let \(P\) be a specified probability law, and let \(L_T\) be measurable under \(P\) for each \(T\in\mathcal T\). A finite-time guarantee supplies deterministic bounds at the stated horizons, for example
\[\forall T\in\mathcal T,\qquad \mathbb E_P[L_T]\le b_T,\]
or, for each \(\delta\in(0,1)\),
\[\forall T\in\mathcal T,\qquad P(L_T\le b_T(\delta))\ge1-\delta.\]
These are pointwise-in-time probability statements. A time-uniform guarantee instead has the form
\[P\!\left(\forall T\in\mathcal T:\ L_T\le b_T(\delta)\right)\ge1-\delta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-time guarantee gives a quantitative bound at each specified finite horizon. Separate per-horizon probability statements are pointwise in time, while a time-uniform guarantee controls every stated horizon on one high-probability event.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Time Guarantees

source_witnesses.source_title: Approximate Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why fixed-horizon validity does not authorize data-dependent horizon selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Separate statements \(P(E_T)\ge1-\delta\) for every deterministic \(T\) do not imply \(P(E_\tau)\ge1-\delta\) for a data-dependent stopping time \(\tau\). Such use requires a simultaneous event, confidence spending, or another anytime-valid argument; repeatedly reusing the full error budget can make the probability of at least one failure exceed \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-horizon bound cannot automatically be reported after inspecting the data and choosing when to stop.
assumptions_latex: The selected horizon may depend on observations used to evaluate the event.

notation.meaning: success event at deterministic horizon T

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Horizon Validity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy-confidence form of a monotone finite-time bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(b_T(\delta)\) is nonincreasing in \(T\) and \(P(L_T\le b_T(\delta))\ge1-\delta\). Define \[N(\epsilon,\delta)=\inf\{T\in\mathbb N:b_T(\delta)\le\epsilon\}.\] If this is finite, every \(T\ge N(\epsilon,\delta)\) satisfies \(P(L_T\le\epsilon)\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone finite-time error bound can be inverted into the evaluation count required for a requested accuracy and confidence.
assumptions_latex: \(b_T(\delta)\) is nonincreasing in \(T\).
The pointwise finite-time bound holds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union-bound construction of simultaneous finite-time validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite or countable \(\mathcal T\), if \(P(L_T>b_T(\delta_T))\le\delta_T\) for each \(T\in\mathcal T\) and \(\sum_{T\in\mathcal T}\delta_T\le\delta\), then \[P\!\left(\forall T\in\mathcal T:L_T\le b_T(\delta_T)\right)\ge1-\delta.\] For \(|\mathcal T|=K<\infty\), \(\delta_T=\delta/K\) is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spending a total error budget across horizons converts pointwise bounds into one simultaneous guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is finite or countable.
Every pointwise bound is valid under the same probability law.

children.title: Asymptotic Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Eventual performance behavior as the evaluation horizon grows.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexamples to missing reverse implications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(L_T=T\mathbf1\{U\le1/T\}\) converges almost surely to zero but \(\mathbb E[L_T]=1\). Separately, for independent events \(A_T\) with \(P(A_T)=1/T\), \(M_T=\mathbf1_{A_T}\) converges to zero in probability but equals one infinitely often almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-sure convergence need not imply mean convergence, and convergence in probability need not imply almost-sure convergence.
assumptions_latex: The events in the second construction are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation of Convergence Modes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Borel-Cantelli criterion for loss convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If for every positive rational \(\epsilon\), \[\sum_{T=1}^{\infty}P(L_T>\epsilon)<\infty,\] then \(L_T\to0\) almost surely. Independence is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable exceedance probabilities at all positive rational tolerances imply almost-sure consistency.
assumptions_latex: Each \(L_T\) is measurable and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Summable-Tail Almost-Sure Consistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic implications and upgrade conditions for nonnegative losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative measurable \(L_T\): \(\mathbb E[L_T]\to0\) implies \(L_T\to0\) in probability, and almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability. If \(L_T\to0\) in probability and \(\{L_T\}\) is uniformly integrable, then \(\mathbb E[L_T]\to0\). In particular, almost-sure convergence plus \(0\le L_T\le Z\) for integrable \(Z\) implies mean convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean and almost-sure convergence each imply convergence in probability; uniform integrability or domination supplies standard upgrades to mean convergence.
assumptions_latex: Each \(L_T\) is nonnegative and measurable.
Integrability, uniform integrability, or domination is assumed where invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L^1\Rightarrow P,\qquad a.s.\Rightarrow P,\qquad P+UI\Rightarrow L^1.
knowledge_statements.title: Implications Among Asymptotic Modes

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathscr A,P)\) is a probability space.
For every \(T\in\mathbb N\), \(L_T:\Omega\to[0,\infty)\) is measurable; integrability is additionally required for the expectation mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The specified convergence mode sends \(L_T\) to \(0\) as \(T\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: probability space supporting the loss sequence

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard convergence-mode taxonomy for nonnegative stochastic losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit behavior of loss or recommendations as evaluations grow without bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\mathscr A,P)\) be a probability space and let \(L_T:\Omega\to[0,\infty)\) be measurable for every \(T\in\mathbb N\). An asymptotic guarantee states a limiting property as \(T\to\infty\). Common forms are expectation consistency,
\[\mathbb E_P[L_T]\to0,\]
when every \(L_T\) is integrable; consistency in probability,
\[\forall\epsilon>0,\qquad P(L_T>\epsilon)\to0;\]
and almost-sure consistency,
\[P\!\left(\lim_{T\to\infty}L_T=0\right)=1.\]
These convergence modes are distinct without additional assumptions, and none alone specifies a finite-horizon rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymptotic guarantee states convergence as the evaluation horizon diverges. Convergence in expectation, in probability, and almost surely are distinct modes and do not by themselves supply finite-time rates.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Guarantees

children.title: Finite-Horizon versus Limit Behavior
children.top_down_role: Compatibility boundaries between finite-time rates and limiting conclusions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Confidence Pointwise Bounds Need Not Imply Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure with nonvanishing pointwise error probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\delta\in(0,1)\), let \(L_T\) be independent Bernoulli\((\delta)\), and set \(b_T=0\). Then \(P(L_T\le b_T)=1-\delta\) for every \(T\), but \(P(L_T>0)=\delta\) never vanishes and \(L_T=1\) infinitely often almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeating the same pointwise fixed-confidence guarantee does not imply convergence in probability or almost-sure consistency.
assumptions_latex: The losses are independent Bernoulli variables with fixed parameter \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Confidence Pointwise Bounds Need Not Imply Consistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of nonasymptotic tail bounds into stochastic consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(b_T\to0\) and \(P(L_T>b_T)\le\delta_T\). If \(\delta_T\to0\), then \(L_T\to0\) in probability. If \(\sum_T\delta_T<\infty\), then \(L_T\le b_T\) eventually almost surely and hence \(L_T\to0\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing bounds and failure probabilities give convergence in probability; summable failure probabilities give almost-sure convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(L_T\ge0\) is measurable.
\(b_T\ge0\) and \(b_T\to0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Tail Bounds to Limit Behavior

assumptions_latex: \((a_T)_{T\ge1}\) is positive and satisfies \(a_T\to0\).
\((L_T)_{T\ge1}\) and \((b_T)_{T\ge1}\) are nonnegative deterministic sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_T\to0\) does not imply \(L_T\le a_T\) eventually for an arbitrarily prescribed \(a_T\to0\); if \(L_T\le b_T\) for every \(T\) and \(b_T\to0\), then \(L_T\to0\).

notation.meaning: arbitrarily prescribed positive vanishing comparison sequence

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary sequence comparison establishes the finite-time versus limit-behavior boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between nonasymptotic rates and convergence-only claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Asymptotic consistency does not determine a prescribed finite-time rate. For any positive sequence \((a_T)_{T\ge1}\) with \(a_T\to0\), the deterministic sequence \(L_T=\sqrt{a_T}\) satisfies \(L_T\to0\) but \(L_T>a_T\) whenever \(0<a_T<1\). Conversely, if nonnegative deterministic sequences satisfy
\[\forall T\in\mathbb N,\qquad L_T\le b_T\]
and \(b_T\to0\), then \(L_T\to0\). If \(\limsup_{T\to\infty}b_T>0\), the inequalities alone do not imply convergence, although convergence may still hold for other reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence alone does not guarantee any arbitrarily prescribed finite-time rate. A vanishing finite-time upper bound does imply convergence, while a nonvanishing upper bound alone gives no convergence conclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon versus Limit Behavior

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be an index set, let \(m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be positive semidefinite. The correctly specified Gaussian-process sample-path regime holds when
\[F\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k),\qquad Y_t=F(X_t)+\varepsilon_t,\]
and the joint prior, observation-noise law, and fixed model parameters used by the policy equal their data-generating counterparts. Guarantees in this regime may average over \(F\) or hold with stated prior probability. They do not thereby become fixed-function guarantees uniformly over the RKHS induced by \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the correctly specified Gaussian-process sample-path regime, the objective is drawn from the Gaussian process used by the policy and the assumed observation law and fixed model parameters match the data-generating ones. Its Bayesian guarantees are not automatically uniform fixed-function RKHS guarantees.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite-Rank Gaussian Draws Lie Outside the Cameron–Martin RKHS
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of a Gaussian sample-path regime from the fixed-function covariance-RKHS regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a Gaussian random element in a separable Hilbert space with covariance eigenpairs \((\lambda_j,\phi_j)\), infinitely many \(\lambda_j>0\), and expansion \[F=\sum_{j\ge1}\sqrt{\lambda_j}Z_j\phi_j,\qquad Z_j\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1).\] Its Cameron–Martin space consists of \(g=\sum_j a_j\phi_j\) with \(\sum_j a_j^2/\lambda_j<\infty\). Membership of \(F\) would require \(\sum_j Z_j^2<\infty\), which fails almost surely; hence \(\mathbb P(F\in\mathcal H_k)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite-rank Gaussian random element almost surely lies outside its covariance Cameron–Martin RKHS, separating Bayesian sample-path and bounded-RKHS regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a Gaussian random element in a separable Hilbert space.
Its covariance operator has infinitely many positive eigenvalues.
\(\mathcal H_k\) denotes the associated Cameron–Martin RKHS.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Rank Gaussian Draws Lie Outside the Cameron–Martin RKHS

children.title: RKHS Objective Regime
children.top_down_role: Frequentist theory for fixed objectives in kernel-induced classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable sufficient membership and norm certificate for finite kernel expansions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \[f(\cdot)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i k(x_i,\cdot),\] then \(f\in\mathcal H_k\) and \[\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}^2=\alpha^\top K\alpha,\qquad K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j).\] Consequently, \(\alpha^\top K\alpha\le B^2\) certifies membership in the radius-\(B\) RKHS ball. On an infinite domain, RKHS membership need not admit a finite expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite kernel expansion belongs to the RKHS, and its Gram quadratic form certifies its norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a fixed-function RKHS guarantee, \(f\in\mathcal H_k\) is nonrandom and satisfies a declared norm bound. This differs from a Bayesian guarantee that averages over a Gaussian-process draw of the objective.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise and increment control implied by a bounded RKHS norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\in\mathcal H_k\), \[f(x)=\langle f,k(x,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal H_k},\qquad |f(x)|\le\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\sqrt{k(x,x)}.\] With \[d_k(x,x')=\sqrt{k(x,x)+k(x',x')-2k(x,x')},\] one also has \[|f(x)-f(x')|\le\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}d_k(x,x').\] Thus a radius-\(B\) objective is \(B\)-Lipschitz in the kernel pseudometric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded RKHS norm controls point values and makes the objective Lipschitz in the kernel-induced pseudometric.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is a real positive-semidefinite kernel.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-function kernel regime underlying frequentist Bayesian-optimization bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a nonempty set, let \(k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be positive semidefinite, and let \(\mathcal H_k\) be its reproducing-kernel Hilbert space. For \(B\in[0,\infty)\), the radius-\(B\) RKHS objective regime is
\[f\in\mathcal H_k\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B,\]
where \(f\) is fixed and observations satisfy \(Y_t=f(X_t)+\varepsilon_t\) under a specified noise law. Probability statements are taken over the observation noise and any policy randomization, not over a Gaussian-process draw of \(f\). A guarantee depending on \(B\) requires a specified valid upper bound on \(\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a fixed member of a bounded ball in the kernel's RKHS. Randomness comes from the specified observation-noise law and any policy randomization, rather than from a Gaussian-process draw of the objective.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: RKHS Norm, Posterior-Mean Identity, and Bounded Objective Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates RKHS complexity to exact centered Gaussian-process regression and defines the bounded RKHS class used in worst-case analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D=(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\) be exact observations for a centered Gaussian process with covariance kernel \(K\), let \(\Sigma=K(\mathbf x,\mathbf x)\) be invertible, and let \(\mu_{\mathcal D}(x)=K(x,\mathbf x)\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf y\). Then \[\|\mu_{\mathcal D}\|_{\mathcal H_K}^2=\mathbf y^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf y.\] For \(B\ge0\), the radius-\(B\) RKHS objective class is \[\mathcal H_K[B]=\{f\in\mathcal H_K:\|f\|_{\mathcal H_K}\le B\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For exact centered-GP regression with an invertible covariance matrix, the posterior mean's squared RKHS norm equals the observations' squared Mahalanobis norm. The radius-B RKHS ball contains the functions whose RKHS norm is at most B.

\Sigma=K(\mathbf x,\mathbf x)\text{ is invertible}
B\ge0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\mu_{\mathcal D}\|_{\mathcal H_K}^2=\mathbf y^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf y,\qquad \mathcal H_K[B]=\{f\in\mathcal H_K:\|f\|_{\mathcal H_K}\le B\}
