knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-design bound for a continuous objective through its modulus of continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be compact, let \(f\in C(\mathcal X)\), and define \[\omega_f(r)=\sup\{|f(x)-f(x')|:d(x,x')\le r\}.\] For sites \(X_1,\ldots,X_T\) with fill distance \(h_T\), any best evaluated site \(\widehat X_T\) satisfies \[0\le \max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)-f(\widehat X_T)\le\omega_f(h_T).\] Hence \(h_T\to0\) implies vanishing noiseless simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The noiseless simple regret of the best sampled point is bounded by the objective's modulus of continuity at the design fill distance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological regime supporting global consistency through compactness and design coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a compact metric space, let \(f\in C(\mathcal X)\), and let \((X_t)_{t\ge1}\subseteq\mathcal X\) have fill distance
\[h_T=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\min_{1\le t\le T}d(x,X_t)\]
satisfying \(h_T\to0\). These conditions define the continuous-objective coverage regime. In the noiseless case, if
\[\widehat X_T\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\{X_1,\ldots,X_T\}}f(x),\]
then
\[\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)-f(\widehat X_T)\to0.\]
With noisy observations, continuity and coverage alone are insufficient; an additional condition controlling value-estimation error, such as suitable replication and uniform consistency, is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime consists of a continuous objective on a compact metric space and evaluated sites whose fill distance vanishes. In the noiseless case, the best evaluated site is globally consistent; noisy observations require an additional condition controlling estimation error.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypothesis Failure Is Not a Robustness Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary after an objective leaves the kernel class assumed by a theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a theorem asserts \(P(f)\Rightarrow Q(f,A)\), where \(P(f)\) includes \(f\in\mathcal H_k\) and \(\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B\). If the true objective violates \(P\), that theorem provides no conclusion about \(Q(f,A)\). A quantitative misspecification guarantee requires an additional premise, such as a certified approximation radius and a transfer theorem; posterior computability alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an RKHS hypothesis fails, the original theorem becomes inapplicable rather than approximately valid; robustness requires a separate quantified premise.
assumptions_latex: The original guarantee explicitly assumes bounded RKHS membership.
No separate misspecification-robust theorem is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \neg P(f)\Longrightarrow\bigl(P(f)\Rightarrow Q(f,A)\bigr)\text{ supplies no guarantee for }f.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypothesis Failure Is Not a Robustness Guarantee

knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-horizon failure for deterministic sequential optimization without regularity or approximation control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=[0,1]\) and let \(A\) be a deterministic sequential policy under noiseless observations, including deterministic recommendations \(\widehat x_T\). Run \(A\) against the zero objective and let \(S\) be the countable union of all queried points and finite-horizon recommendations on that history. Choose \(x^\star\in\mathcal X\setminus S\) and set \(f(x)=\mathbf 1\{x=x^\star\}\). The observations remain identical to the zero-objective history, so every query and recommendation stays in \(S\). Consequently, for every \(T\ge1\), \[f(x^\star)-\max_{1\le t\le T}f(x_t)=1,\qquad f(x^\star)-f(\widehat x_T)=1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any deterministic policy on an uncountable domain, an unrestricted spike objective can be placed outside every query and recommendation, leaving simple regret one at every horizon.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X=[0,1]\).
The policy and its recommendation rule are deterministic.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of kernel-class guarantees when the objective lacks controlled representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An RKHS-based guarantee whose hypotheses require \(f\in\mathcal H_k\) and \(\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B\) does not apply when neither a finite valid radius nor a controlled approximation error is available. For a concrete failure boundary, let \(\mathcal X=[0,1]\), let \(k(x,x')=1\), and let \(f(x)=x\). The RKHS \(\mathcal H_k\) contains only constant functions, so \(f\notin\mathcal H_k\). Consider noiseless observations and a policy whose acquisition at each round depends only on the modeled posterior marginal mean and variance. Under the constant-kernel model these marginal quantities are identical at every \(x\in[0,1]\); if every acquisition tie is resolved at \(0\), the policy may select \(X_t=0\) for all \(t\). Its simple regret
\[r_T=\max_{x\in[0,1]}f(x)-\max_{1\le t\le T}f(X_t)\]
then satisfies \(r_T=1\) for every \(T\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An RKHS guarantee is inapplicable when its representability hypothesis fails. With a constant-kernel model, the true objective f(x)=x lies outside the model class, and a posterior-marginal acquisition policy that always breaks ties at zero can sample zero forever and retain simple regret one.
knowledge_statements.title: Model-Class Misspecification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural laws for uniform distance to a bounded RKHS model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\rho_{k,B}(f)=\inf_{\|g\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B}\|f-g\|_\infty,\] whenever the uniform norms are finite, \[B_1\le B_2\Rightarrow \rho_{k,B_2}(f)\le\rho_{k,B_1}(f),\qquad |\rho_{k,B}(f)-\rho_{k,B}(f')|\le\|f-f'\|_\infty.\] Moreover, \(\rho_{k,B}(f)=0\) exactly when \(f\) lies in the uniform closure of the radius-\(B\) RKHS ball; an attaining RKHS witness need not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation error decreases with RKHS budget, is Lipschitz in the objective, and vanishes exactly on the uniform closure of the bounded model class.
assumptions_latex: The objectives have finite uniform norm.
\(k\) is positive semidefinite and all radii are nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided certificate for a declared uniform approximation tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(g\in\mathcal H_k\) satisfying \(\|g\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B\), a verified full-domain residual bound \(\|f-g\|_\infty\le r\) certifies \[\rho_{k,B}(f)\le r.\] This remains sound when the infimum defining \(\rho_{k,B}(f)\) is not attained. Failure to find such a witness does not certify \(\rho_{k,B}(f)>r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-RKHS witness with a verified full-domain residual gives a sound upper bound on approximation radius; failure to find one proves no lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(g\in\mathcal H_k\) and \(\|g\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of empirical residual checks on a strict subset of the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subsetneq\mathcal X\) be finite. In general, \[\max_{x\in S}|f(x)-g(x)|\le r\] does not imply \(\|f-g\|_\infty\le r\) or \(\rho_{k,B}(f)\le r\). Without regularity connecting unsampled points to \(S\), an objective can agree with \(g\) on \(S\) and differ arbitrarily at a point of \(\mathcal X\setminus S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small sampled residuals do not certify uniform kernel representability without an off-design regularity and covering argument.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho_{k,B}(f)=\inf_{\|g\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B}\|f-g\|_\infty\), every \(c>0\) satisfies \[\rho_{k,cB}(cf)=c\rho_{k,B}(f),\qquad \rho_{k,0}(f)=\|f\|_\infty.\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational procedure induced by the exact finite-domain representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(\mathcal X\), compute \(K\) and \(f_X\), impose \(v\in\operatorname{range}(K)\), and minimize \(r\) subject to \(-r\mathbf1\le f_X-v\le r\mathbf1\) and \(v^\top K^\dagger v\le B^2\). Any feasible pair \((v,r)\) certifies \(\rho_{k,B}(f)\le r\); an exact optimizer returns the finite-domain approximation radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-domain approximation radius can be computed by a convex quadratic-cone program, and every feasible solution provides an upper certificate.
assumptions_latex: The finite-domain objective vector and kernel Gram matrix are available.
Equality requires an exact optimizer; approximate solves provide solver-qualified bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Domain Convex Representation of the Approximation Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional formulation when the search domain is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\), let \(K=(k(x_i,x_j))_{i,j}\succeq0\), and let \(f_X=(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n))\). Then \[\rho_{k,B}(f)=\min_{v,r}\left\{r:\ -r\mathbf1\le f_X-v\le r\mathbf1,\ v\in\operatorname{range}(K),\ v^\top K^\dagger v\le B^2\right\}.\] If \(K\succ0\), the range constraint is redundant and \(K^\dagger=K^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite domain, uniform distance to an RKHS ball is exactly a convex quadratic-cone problem over the modeled value vector.
assumptions_latex: The search domain is the displayed finite set.
\(K\) is the positive-semidefinite kernel Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_{k,B}(f)=\min\{r:-r\mathbf1\le f_X-v\le r\mathbf1,\ v\in\operatorname{range}(K),\ v^\top K^\dagger v\le B^2\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment-safe definition of uniform proximity to a bounded kernel model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a positive-semidefinite kernel \(k\) with RKHS \(\mathcal H_k\), define \[\rho_{k,B}(f):=\inf_{\substack{g\in\mathcal H_k\\\|g\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B}}\|f-g\|_\infty.\] The objective is \((k,B,\varepsilon)\)-approximately representable exactly when \(\rho_{k,B}(f)\le\varepsilon\), equivalently when for every \(\eta>0\) there exists \(g_\eta\in\mathcal H_k\) with \(\|g_\eta\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B\) and \(\|f-g_\eta\|_\infty\le\varepsilon+\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate kernel representability is uniform distance at most epsilon from the radius-B RKHS ball, with positive slack allowing for a nonattained infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is positive semidefinite on the nonempty domain \(\mathcal X\).
\(B,\varepsilon\ge0\), and the relevant uniform norms are finite.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the bounded kernel model class by \(\mathcal B_k(B)=\{g\in\mathcal H_k:\lVert g\rVert_{\mathcal H_k}\le B\}\) and its uniform approximation radius by \[\rho_{k,B}(f)=\inf_{g\in\mathcal B_k(B)}\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f(x)-g(x)|.\] The objective \(f\) is \((k,B,\varepsilon)\)-approximately kernel representable if \(\rho_{k,B}(f)\le\varepsilon\); equivalently, for every \(\eta>0\) there exists \(g_\eta\in\mathcal B_k(B)\) such that \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f(x)-g_\eta(x)|\le\varepsilon+\eta\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Two-Radius Simple-Regret Penalty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point construction showing that a general uniform-perturbation constant below two is impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{a,b\}\), \(g(a)=g(b)=0\), and, for \(0<\delta<\varepsilon\), set \[f(a)=\varepsilon,\qquad f(b)=-\varepsilon+\delta.\] Then \(\|f-g\|_\infty\le\varepsilon\). Recommending \(b\) has zero simple regret under \(g\), while its simple regret under \(f\) is \(2\varepsilon-\delta\). Thus the worst-case transfer penalty approaches \(2\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-point example makes the simple-regret transfer penalty arbitrarily close to twice the uniform approximation radius.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
\(0<\delta<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Two-Radius Simple-Regret Penalty

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic transfer of maximization regret under a uniform objective perturbation, stated without requiring attained suprema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be bounded and satisfy \(\|f-g\|_\infty\le\varepsilon\). Define \(r_h(x)=\sup_{z\in\mathcal X}h(z)-h(x)\). Then for every \(x\), \[r_f(x)\le r_g(x)+2\varepsilon.\] Consequently, for every query sequence, \[R_T(f):=\sum_{t=1}^T r_f(x_t)\le R_T(g)+2\varepsilon T.\] For every recommendation \(\widehat x_T\), \(r_f(\widehat x_T)\le r_g(\widehat x_T)+2\varepsilon\). These inequalities hold pathwise and therefore persist under expectations whenever the quantities are integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform objective error epsilon adds at most two epsilon to each instantaneous or terminal regret and at most two epsilon times the horizon to cumulative regret.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are bounded on the same nonempty domain.
\(\|f-g\|_\infty\le\varepsilon\).
Expectation versions additionally require integrability.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(x\in\mathcal X\), uniform approximation gives \[f(x_f^*)-f(x)\le g(x_g^*)-g(x)+2\varepsilon.\] Hence, for arbitrary queries \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\), defining \(R_T(h)=\sum_{t=1}^T(h(x_h^*)-h(x_t))\), one has \[R_T(f)\le R_T(g)+2\varepsilon T.\] If an output \(\widehat x_T\) has model simple regret \(g(x_g^*)-g(\widehat x_T)\le r_T\), then its true simple regret satisfies \(f(x_f^*)-f(\widehat x_T)\le r_T+2\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-action regime holds precisely when \(0<K=|\mathcal X|<\infty\). For any objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), a maximizer exists and \[\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le K}f(x^{(i)}).\] Consequently, a simultaneous event formed from actionwise failure events \(E_i\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(\bigcup_{i=1}^K E_i)\le\sum_{i=1}^K\mathbb P(E_i)\); no covering construction or continuity extension is required to obtain uniform control over \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite action domain contains K alternatives, so maxima exist and uniform confidence can be obtained by finite actionwise comparison or union bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous concentration over a finite action set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(K)}\}\). If \(\Pr(|\widehat f_i-f(x^{(i)})|>r_i(\eta))\le\eta\) for every action i, then for \(\delta\in(0,1)\), \[\Pr\!\left(\forall i\le K:\ |\widehat f_i-f(x^{(i)})|\le r_i(\delta/K)\right)\ge1-\delta.\] If each error is \(\sigma_i^2/n_i\)-sub-Gaussian, one may take \[r_i(\delta/K)=\sigma_i\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2K/\delta)}{n_i}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocating failure probability delta/K converts actionwise intervals into simultaneous intervals, with logarithmic dependence on the number of actions under sub-Gaussian noise.

children.title: Compact Continuous Domains
children.top_down_role: Guarantees using continuity, coverings, or metric regularity.

assumptions_latex: The search space \((\mathcal X,d)\) is a nonempty compact metric space.
The objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum is attained, and every positive scale admits a finite covering of \(\mathcal X\).

notation.meaning: metric covering number at radius delta

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact metric-domain regime supporting attainment and finite coverings.

source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The compact continuous-domain regime consists of a nonempty compact metric space \((\mathcal X,d)\) and a continuous objective \(f\). Then there exists \(x^*\in\mathcal X\) satisfying \(f(x^*)=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\). Moreover, for every \(\delta>0\), the covering number is finite: \[N(\mathcal X,d,\delta)<\infty.\] Thus a guarantee proved on a finite \(\delta\)-net can be extended to all of \(\mathcal X\) whenever the objective, posterior process, or confidence bounds have the required modulus of continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact metric domain, continuous objectives attain maxima and finite metric nets exist at every positive resolution.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Continuous Domains

source_witnesses.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness Alone Does Not Bound Discretization Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating finite-cover existence from quantitative finite-net transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compactness guarantees finite \(h\)-nets, but it gives no vanishing bound on \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}g(x)-\max_{u\in D_h}g(u)\) for an arbitrary function \(g\). Quantitative transfer requires a modulus of continuity or comparable regularity for the controlled quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness supplies finite covers, but discretization error requires additional regularity.
assumptions_latex: Only compactness of the domain is assumed; no regularity of \(g\) is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No vanishing discretization-error bound follows from compactness alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Alone Does Not Bound Discretization Error

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic transfer of finite-net value control on a compact metric domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be compact and suppose \(|g(x)-g(x')|\le\omega(d(x,x'))\), where \(\omega(r)\to0\) as \(r\downarrow0\). If \(D_h\) is an \(h\)-net, then \[0\le \sup_{x\in\mathcal X}g(x)-\max_{u\in D_h}g(u)\le\omega(h).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An h-net approximates the maximum of a uniformly continuous function within its modulus of continuity at h.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal X,d)\) is compact.
\(D_h\) is an \(h\)-net.
\(g\) has modulus of continuity \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Continuity Net Transfer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous differentiability implies Lipschitz continuity on a compact convex domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective regularity used in Bayesian-optimization guarantees over compact continuous domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal X\subseteq[0,m]^d be compact and convex. If f is continuously differentiable on \mathcal X, then there exists L<\infty such that \lvert f(x)-f(y)\rvert\le L\lVert x-y\rVert_2 for all x,y\in\mathcal X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable objective on a compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional cube is globally Lipschitz on that domain.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal X\subseteq[0,m]^d\text{ is compact and convex}
f\text{ is continuously differentiable on }\mathcal X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists L<\infty\ \forall x,y\in\mathcal X:\ \lvert f(x)-f(y)\rvert\le L\lVert x-y\rVert_2

children.title: Structured Search Domains
children.top_down_role: Guarantee interfaces for combinatorial, categorical, graph, or non-Euclidean search spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is bijective.
\(\rho(\phi(x),\phi(x'))=d(x,x')\) for all \(x,x'\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Covering numbers and Lipschitz constants are preserved by \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation invariance for structured-domain metric quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\phi:(\mathcal X,d)\to(\mathcal Z,\rho)\) is a bijective isometry, then for every \(\epsilon>0\), \[N(\mathcal X,d,\epsilon)=N(\mathcal Z,\rho,\epsilon),\] and f is L-Lipschitz on \((\mathcal X,d)\) if and only if \(f\circ\phi^{-1}\) is L-Lipschitz on \((\mathcal Z,\rho)\). Guarantees depending only on these quantities are therefore invariant under isometric relabeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isometric encodings preserve covering numbers and Lipschitz constants, so geometry-based guarantees do not depend on arbitrary labels.
knowledge_statements.title: Isometry Invariance of Geometry-Based Guarantees

assumptions_latex: G is an undirected graph.
Every edge length is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weighted shortest-path distance is a metric on each connected component; disconnected components require an additional finite cross-component geometry.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric representation for graph-structured search spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be an undirected graph with strictly positive edge lengths. On each connected component, \[d_G(u,v)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}w_e\] is a metric. If G is disconnected, the same formula is infinite between components and does not define a finite-valued metric on all of V until an explicit cross-component geometry is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive weighted shortest paths define a metric within each connected graph component; disconnected graphs need a separate cross-component distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shortest-Path Geometry on Structured Graph Domains
knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path Geometry on Structured Graph Domains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality capacity bound for finite structured families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((\mathcal X,d)\) is nonempty and finite with \(|\mathcal X|=M\), then \[1\le N(\mathcal X,d,\epsilon)\le M.\] If \(0<\epsilon<\tfrac12\min_{x\ne x'}d(x,x')\), then \(N(\mathcal X,d,\epsilon)=M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite structured family has covering number at most its cardinality, with equality below half its minimum separation.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a nonempty finite metric space.
Covering centers lie in the underlying metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\mathcal X,d,\epsilon)\le|\mathcal X|,\qquad N(\mathcal X,d,\epsilon)=|\mathcal X|\text{ at the stated fine resolution}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Structured-Domain Entropy Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Metrics for Categorical and Combinatorial Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative native geometries for unordered categories, subsets, permutations, and fixed-length sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Representative metrics are the discrete metric \(d(a,b)=\mathbf1\{a\ne b\}\) on unordered labels, symmetric-difference distance \(d(A,B)=|A\triangle B|\) on finite subsets, Kendall distance on permutations, and Hamming distance \(d_H(u,v)=\sum_{i=1}^p\mathbf1\{u_i\ne v_i\}\) on fixed-length sequences. Kendall distance equals the minimum number of adjacent transpositions converting one permutation into the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unordered labels, subsets, permutations, and fixed-length sequences have metrics preserving their native combinatorial structure.
assumptions_latex: Compared objects belong to the same stated structured family.
Sequences have a common finite length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each displayed distance is a metric on its stated domain}.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Metrics for Categorical and Combinatorial Objects

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncontrolled Numeric Encodings Can Destroy Structured Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for transferring geometry-based guarantees through an encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an injective encoding \(\phi:(\mathcal X,d)\to(\mathbb R^q,\|\cdot\|)\), bounds \[c\,d(x,x')\le\|\phi(x)-\phi(x')\|\le C\,d(x,x')\] with \(0<c\le C<\infty\) provide controlled transfer of metric regularity and covering estimates. Without such distortion control, encoded distances, Lipschitz constants, and covering numbers need not control their native counterparts; arbitrary numeric labels for unordered categories can therefore change geometry under a mere relabeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary numeric encodings need not preserve native adjacency, distance, entropy, or regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is an injective representation of structured objects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Uniform geometry-based transfer requires declared distortion control}.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Numeric Encodings Can Destroy Structured Regularity

assumptions_latex: The domain has a known decomposition \(\mathcal X=\bigcup_{s\in\mathcal S}\mathcal X_s\), where \(\mathcal S\) is finite or countable.
Each component \((\mathcal X_s,d_s)\) has a specified geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Search complexity can be controlled componentwise when the weighted component covering sum is finite.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: decomposed search spaces are controlled through componentwise geometry and complexity aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component-decomposed domains with explicitly controlled local complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structured search domain is a decomposition \(\mathcal X=\bigcup_{s\in\mathcal S}\mathcal X_s\) equipped with component metrics \(d_s\) and nonnegative weights \(\pi_s\) satisfying \(\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\pi_s=1\). At resolution \(\delta>0\), its weighted structural complexity is controlled when \[\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\pi_s N(\mathcal X_s,d_s,\delta)<\infty.\] Guarantees may then allocate componentwise failure probabilities \(\alpha_s\) with \(\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\alpha_s\le\alpha\), provided the acquisition rule searches every component retained by the guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured domain is decomposed into geometric components whose covering complexities and confidence budgets can be aggregated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Structured Search Domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted covering-number criterion is a particular construction, not a canonical consequence of a component decomposition, and its precise relevance to search complexity depends on the guarantee. An authoritative source is needed.

children.title: Mixed-Variable Domains
children.top_down_role: Guarantee interfaces for search spaces combining discrete and continuous variables.

assumptions_latex: Every discrete factor \(D_j\) is finite.
Each indicated continuous-factor covering number is finite.
The weights \(a_i,b_j\) are positive and \(\sum_i a_i\epsilon_i\le\epsilon\).

notation.meaning: covering resolution assigned to continuous factor i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covering complexity of continuous factors combined with finite discrete factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[\mathcal X=\prod_{i=1}^{p}C_i\times\prod_{j=1}^{q}D_j\] carry the metric \[d(x,x')=\sum_{i=1}^{p}a_i d_i(x_i,x_i')+\sum_{j=1}^{q}b_j\mathbf 1\{x_{p+j}\ne x'_{p+j}\}.\] For positive \(\epsilon_i\) satisfying \(\sum_i a_i\epsilon_i\le\epsilon\), \[N(\mathcal X,d,\epsilon)\le\left(\prod_{i=1}^{p}N(C_i,d_i,\epsilon_i)\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^{q}|D_j|\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-domain cover combines factorwise continuous covers with enumeration of the finite discrete configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product Covering Bound for Mixed Domains
knowledge_statements.title: Product Covering Bound for Mixed Domains

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a compact metric space.
\(D\) is finite and nonempty.
The metric on \(C\times D\) induces the product topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\times D\) is compact, and every continuous real-valued objective on it attains its maximum and minimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness criterion for a finite-discrete mixed product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If C is a compact metric space and D is a nonempty finite set with the discrete topology, then \(C\times D\) is compact under every product-compatible metric. Consequently, every continuous \(f:C\times D\to\mathbb R\) attains a maximum and a minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite discrete block preserves compactness of a compact continuous block, so continuous objectives attain optima on their mixed product.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness of Finite-Discrete Mixed Products

assumptions_latex: The decision has \(p\ge0\) continuous coordinates and \(q\ge0\) discrete coordinates.
Each continuous factor \(C_i\) is a metric space and each discrete factor \(D_j\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The product metric separates continuous displacement from discrete coordinate changes and defines the mixed-domain covering geometry.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a product of continuous and discrete factors is the canonical mixed-variable domain model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product domains containing continuous and discrete decision coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-variable domain has the form \[\mathcal X=\prod_{i=1}^{p}C_i\times\prod_{j=1}^{q}D_j,\] where each \((C_i,d_i)\) is a metric space and each \(D_j\) carries the discrete metric. For positive weights \(a_i\) and \(b_j\), one compatible product metric is \[d(x,x')=\sum_{i=1}^{p}a_i d_i(x_i,x_i')+\sum_{j=1}^{q}b_j\mathbf 1\{x_{p+j}\ne x'_{p+j}\}.\] A guarantee belongs to this regime only if its covering, kernel, or acquisition assumptions are stated for the resulting product geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-variable domain is a product of continuous and discrete factors equipped with a metric that accounts for both displacement and category changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Variable Domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-domain definition and displayed weighted metric are mathematically valid, but no inspectable source supports the selected mixed-domain formulation or its guarantee-applicability clause.

children.title: Cross-Component Geometry
children.top_down_role: Capacity and regularity effects arising from heterogeneous domain components.

assumptions_latex: The prior is Gaussian and has zero covariance between different components.
Observation errors are independent of the latent process and conditionally independent across observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L(f|_{\mathcal X_s}\mid\text{data outside }\mathcal X_s)=\mathcal L(f|_{\mathcal X_s})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior separation induced by zero cross-component covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Gaussian-process prior have kernel k satisfying \(k(x,x')=0\) whenever x and \(x'\) belong to different components. Under independent observation noise, conditioning on observations collected outside \(\mathcal X_s\) leaves the posterior mean and covariance on \(\mathcal X_s\) unchanged. Observations in one component therefore cannot reduce latent uncertainty in another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-diagonal kernel makes distinct components posterior-independent, so observations in one component cannot reduce uncertainty in another.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block-Diagonal Kernels Do Not Transfer Information Across Components
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Diagonal Kernels Do Not Transfer Information Across Components

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many nonempty components.
The global metric separates every pair of distinct components by at least \(\rho>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric entropy of finitely many mutually separated components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)=\bigsqcup_{s=1}^{m}\mathcal X_s\), and suppose \[\rho=\min_{s\ne t}\inf\{d(x,x'):x\in\mathcal X_s,\ x'\in\mathcal X_t\}>0.\] For every \(0<\epsilon<\rho/2\), \[N(\mathcal X,d,\epsilon)=\sum_{s=1}^{m}N(\mathcal X_s,d|_{\mathcal X_s},\epsilon).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Below half the minimum inter-component separation, every global cover decomposes exactly into separate component covers.
knowledge_statements.title: Separated-Component Covering Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariance geometry specified through within- and between-component kernel blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal X=\bigsqcup_{s=1}^m\mathcal X_s\), let \(k_{st}:\mathcal X_s\times\mathcal X_t\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(k_{st}(x,x')=k_{ts}(x',x)\). The assembled function \(k\) is a covariance kernel on \(\mathcal X\) exactly when, for every finite collection, \[\sum_{s,t=1}^m\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\sum_{j=1}^{n_t}a_{si}a_{tj}k_{st}(x_{si},x_{tj})\ge0.\] Diagonal blocks describe within-component covariance, while off-diagonal blocks determine cross-component information transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid cross-component covariance model is a jointly positive-semidefinite block kernel whose off-diagonal blocks determine information transfer.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a finite disjoint union of nonempty components.
The assembled kernel is real-valued and symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\text{ is a covariance kernel on }\mathcal X\iff k\text{ satisfies joint positive semidefiniteness}.

notation.meaning: covariance block between components s and t

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Component Kernel Coupling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise Kernel Compatibility Does Not Ensure Global Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint positive-semidefiniteness boundary for cross-component covariance blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On three singleton components, consider \[K=\begin{pmatrix}1&r&r\\r&1&-r\\r&-r&1\end{pmatrix}.\] For \(|r|\le1\), every one- and two-component principal block is positive semidefinite, but \(\det K=1-3r^2-2r^3<0\) at \(r=3/4\). Thus componentwise and pairwise validity do not imply validity of the full block kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally and pairwise valid covariance blocks need not form a valid global covariance kernel.
assumptions_latex: The three components are singletons.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Kernel Compatibility Does Not Ensure Global Validity

assumptions_latex: The domain is a disjoint union \(\mathcal X=\bigsqcup_{s\in\mathcal S}\mathcal X_s\).
Each component has an internal metric \(d_s\), and \(\Delta\) is a metric on \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid global geometry must control both within-component distances and distances between component labels.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: disconnected or conditional components require an explicit inter-component geometry
source needed for the selected metric construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry coupling distances within and between structural components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose reference points \(o_s\in\mathcal X_s\) and define, for \(x\in\mathcal X_s\) and \(x'\in\mathcal X_t\), \[d(x,x')=\begin{cases}d_s(x,x'),&s=t,\\ d_s(x,o_s)+\Delta(s,t)+d_t(o_t,x'),&s\ne t.\end{cases}\] This path construction is a metric when every \(d_s\) and \(\Delta\) is a metric. Cross-component guarantee calculations must use the resulting global covering numbers or a kernel defined on this geometry; componentwise regularity alone does not control comparisons across distinct components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-component geometry combines each component's internal metric with explicit distances between component labels, enabling global coverings and comparisons.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Component Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reference-point path construction does define a metric under the stated metric assumptions, but the chosen construction and its asserted role in guarantee calculations lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Noncompact-Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Localization and existence issues on unbounded search spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact-Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of maximizer existence without compactness or localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the noncompact domain \(\mathcal X=\mathbb R\), the continuous bounded objective \(f(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\) satisfies \(\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)=1\), but no \(x^*\in\mathbb R\) attains this value. Therefore a guarantee written using \(f(x^*)\) is not well posed on arbitrary noncompact domains. It becomes applicable only after replacing attainment by supremum-based regret or imposing a condition such as a known compact localization set containing an optimizer, an attainment assumption, or a high-probability localization argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a noncompact domain, even a continuous bounded objective may have no maximizer; guarantees require supremum-based regret or an explicit attainment or localization condition.
assumptions_latex: The search domain \(\mathcal X\) is noncompact.
No compact localization set or attainment assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite supremum need not be attained, so regret defined relative to a maximizer may be undefined.

notation.meaning: noncompact search domain in the counterexample
continuous bounded objective in the counterexample

source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit continuous bounded counterexample directly demonstrates failure of attainment

source_witnesses.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a topological space.
\(f\) is upper semicontinuous.
For some \(x_0\in\mathcal X\), the upper-level set \(L_{x_0}\) is nonempty and compact.

notation.meaning: compact upper-level localization set determined by x0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient optimizer-localization condition on a noncompact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be upper semicontinuous. If some \(x_0\in\mathcal X\) has a nonempty compact upper-level set \[L_{x_0}=\{x\in\mathcal X:f(x)\ge f(x_0)\},\] then f attains its global maximum and \(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)=\max_{x\in L_{x_0}}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-semicontinuous objective on a noncompact domain attains its maximum if one nonempty upper-level set is compact.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Upper-Level Localization Ensures Attainment

assumptions_latex: The nonempty compact sets \(K_m\) are nested and satisfy \(\bigcup_{m\ge1}K_m=\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\sup_{x\in K_m}f(x)\), with no implied convergence rate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supremum approximation through expanding compact subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal X\) are nonempty compact sets with \(\bigcup_{m\ge1}K_m=\mathcal X\). For any \(f:\mathcal X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \[\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\sup_{x\in K_m}f(x).\] This identity supplies no finite-m localization error bound without an additional tail, coercivity, or optimizer-location condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested compact searches that exhaust the domain recover the global supremum, but noncompactness alone provides no rate or finite localization error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustion by Compact Localization Sets

children.title: Exact Observations
children.top_down_role: Deterministic evaluation regime underlying classical efficient global optimization.

assumptions_latex: At round \(t\), the learner selects \(x_t\in\mathcal X\).
Evaluation of the deterministic objective \(f\) introduces no measurement or simulation error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The observation satisfies \(y_t=f(x_t)\) almost surely and has zero conditional variance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noise-free sequential evaluation of a deterministic objective.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Observations and data in stochastic optimization p. 62
source_refs.source_title: Reinforcement Learning and Stochastic Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact-observation regime is defined by \[y_t=f(x_t)\quad\text{almost surely for every }t.\] Equivalently, with observation error \(\varepsilon_t=y_t-f(x_t)\), one has \(\varepsilon_t=0\) almost surely, and therefore \(\mathbb E[y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=f(x_t)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t)=0\). Replication at the same input yields the same value and cannot reduce any epistemic uncertainty arising solely from unsampled locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact feedback returns the objective value without error, giving zero conditional observation variance at every queried point.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Observations

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.1 Observations and data in stochastic optimization p. 62
source_witnesses.source_title: Reinforcement Learning and Stochastic Optimization

assumptions_latex: S is a proper finite subset of \(\mathcal X\).
No regularity class constrains objective values away from sampled points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact agreement on all observed data does not determine whether an unsampled point is globally better.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indistinguishability of unsampled objective values without regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subsetneq\mathcal X\) be any finite sampled set and choose \(z\in\mathcal X\setminus S\). There exist objectives \(f,g:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(f(x)=g(x)\) for every \(x\in S\), while \(g(z)>\sup_{x\in S}g(x)\) and \(f(z)<\sup_{x\in S}f(x)\). Exact observations on S therefore cannot by themselves certify that the best sampled point is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noise-free values at finitely many points leave arbitrary unsampled improvements possible unless regularity or exhaustive coverage is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Feedback Alone Does Not Certify Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Feedback Alone Does Not Certify Global Optimality

assumptions_latex: Observations are exact.
The queried inputs are distinct.
The kernel Gram matrix is invertible.

notation.meaning: kernel Gram matrix at observed inputs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior interpolation at distinct exactly observed inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\), and observe \(y_i=f(x_i)\) exactly at distinct inputs. If \(K_n=[k(x_i,x_j)]_{i,j}\) is invertible, then the noiseless posterior satisfies \(\mu_n(x_i)=y_i\) and \(k_n(x_i,x_i)=0\) for every observed input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an invertible Gram matrix and zero observation noise, the GP posterior interpolates every observation and has zero latent variance there.
knowledge_statements.title: Noiseless Gaussian-Process Interpolation

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory covers exact-feedback equivalences, deterministic replication, zero observation variance, and the failure of exact samples alone to certify a global optimum. Noisy concentration belongs to feedback siblings; noiseless GP interpolation belongs to posterior representation; acquisition design and deterministic solver certificates remain in their dedicated leaves.

children.title: Light-Tailed Independent Noise
children.top_down_role: Canonical noisy-feedback regime for GP-bandit concentration analysis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample confidence radius for independent uniformly sub-Gaussian replication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n\) are independent, centered, and \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian, then \(n^{-1}\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) is \(\sigma/\sqrt n\)-sub-Gaussian and \[\Pr\!\left(\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i\right|>\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2/\delta)}{n}}\right)\le\delta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging independent sub-Gaussian errors reduces the confidence radius at the square-root-n rate.
assumptions_latex: Errors are mutually independent, centered, and share sub-Gaussian scale \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration of Independent Replicate Means

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Light Tails Do Not Imply Independent-Round Concentration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence boundary for independent-noise guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be centered and \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian, and set \(\varepsilon_t=Z\) for every \(t\). Every marginal error is \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian, but \(n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\varepsilon_t=Z\), so averaging produces no \(n^{-1/2}\) improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfectly dependent sub-Gaussian errors receive no concentration gain from averaging.
assumptions_latex: A single centered sub-Gaussian variable is reused at every round.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Light Tails Do Not Imply Independent-Round Concentration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of a common sub-Gaussian MGF scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If centered \(\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\mathbb E e^{\lambda\varepsilon}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\) for all \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), then \[\Pr(|\varepsilon|\ge u)\le2e^{-u^2/(2\sigma^2)}.\] All polynomial moments are finite and \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sub-Gaussian MGF bound yields Gaussian-type tails, all polynomial moments, and variance bounded by the squared scale.
assumptions_latex: The centered error obeys the stated MGF bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Sub-Gaussian Tail and Moment Consequences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Innovation formulation of light-tailed feedback under adaptive querying.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_t\) be \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable. Suppose \(U_t\) is independent of \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\) and \[Y_t=f(x_t)+h_t(x_t,U_t),\qquad \mathbb E[h_t(x,U_t)]=0,\qquad\sup_{t,x}\|h_t(x,U_t)\|_{\psi_2}\le K.\] When the innovations are mutually independent and the history contains all earlier observations and algorithmic randomization, this gives fresh, uniformly light-tailed one-step errors despite adaptive query selection. It does not assert factorization after conditioning on the entire future adaptively selected query sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive light-tailed feedback can be generated from fresh independent innovations passed through uniformly sub-Gaussian query-dependent error maps.
assumptions_latex: Queries are predictable.
Each innovation is fresh relative to the pre-observation history, and the innovation sequence is mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Fresh Sub-Gaussian Innovation Representation

assumptions_latex: The query \(x_t\) is measurable with respect to the past information \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\).
The noise variables are conditionally independent given the query sequence and share a finite sub-Gaussian scale \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each centered observation error obeys the conditional moment-generating-function bound \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda\varepsilon_t}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\).
review_flags: locator may discuss observations more generally than conditional sub-Gaussian noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditionally independent, uniformly sub-Gaussian observation errors.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Observations and data in stochastic optimization p. 62
source_refs.source_title: Reinforcement Learning and Stochastic Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Observations have the form \(y_t=f(x_t)+\varepsilon_t\), where \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0\). The light-tailed condition requires a constant \(\sigma<\infty\) such that, for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), \[\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda\varepsilon_t)\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le\exp(\lambda^2\sigma^2/2)\quad\text{almost surely}.\] Conditional independence means that, given the selected queries, the joint conditional law of the errors factors into their one-round conditional laws. This regime supports exponential concentration uniformly across adaptive rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Light-tailed independent feedback has centered, conditionally independent errors with a common sub-Gaussian moment-generating-function bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Light-Tailed Independent Noise

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Heteroscedasticity Does Not Imply Light Tails
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of input-dependent variance from tail assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) have a centered Student distribution with three degrees of freedom and let \(\varepsilon(x)=s(x)T\), where \(s(x)>0\) is nonconstant. Then \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon(x))=3s^2(x)\) is finite and nonconstant, while \(\mathbb E e^{\lambda\varepsilon(x)}=\infty\) for every \(\lambda\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconstant finite variance function can coexist with heavy-tailed, non-sub-Gaussian errors.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is centered Student-t with three degrees of freedom.
\(s\) is positive and nonconstant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon(x))=3s^2(x)\text{ and the nonzero MGF is infinite}.
knowledge_statements.title: Heteroscedasticity Does Not Imply Light Tails

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-moment definition of input-dependent observation variability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Y_t=f(x_t)+\varepsilon_t\), suppose \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t)=v(x_t)\). The feedback is heteroscedastic when \(v\) is nonconstant on the query domain. This variance formulation alone implies neither Gaussian nor sub-Gaussian tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heteroscedastic noise has a nonconstant conditional variance function, without necessarily having light tails.
assumptions_latex: Conditional second moments exist.
Given the query, the conditional variance is the deterministic function \(v(x_t)\), not an additional function of history.
The latent objective is fixed over evaluation time.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Variance-Function Formulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Location-specific variance reduction from independent replication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(r\) conditionally independent observations at \(x\) have common conditional variance \(v(x)\), their average satisfies \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_r(x)\mid x)=\frac{v(x)}{r}.\] Equal replication counts therefore generally give unequal precision across locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent replication divides local variance by the replicate count, so equal replication need not equalize precision.
assumptions_latex: Replicates at x are conditionally independent with common finite variance \(v(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Replication Precision Under Heteroscedastic Noise

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-data likelihood under independent Gaussian heteroscedastic errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), independent Gaussian errors with variances \(v(x_i)\) give \[Y\mid f,X\sim\mathcal N(f_X,D_X),\qquad D_X=\operatorname{diag}(v(x_1),\ldots,v(x_n)).\] Under a GP prior with Gram matrix \(K\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y\mid X)=K+D_X\). Replacing \(D_X\) by \(\sigma^2I\) is exact only in the homoscedastic case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent Gaussian heteroscedastic observations use an input-dependent diagonal noise matrix added to latent covariance.
assumptions_latex: Errors are conditionally independent and Gaussian.
Every \(v(x_i)\) is finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Heteroscedastic Likelihood

assumptions_latex: Observations satisfy \(y_t=f(x_t)+\varepsilon_t\).
The scale function \(\sigma:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)\) is finite on the search domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Observation uncertainty depends on the queried input through \(\sigma(x_t)\), rather than a single constant scale.
review_flags: source for the input-dependent conditional bound is indirect
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditionally centered noise with input-dependent scale.

source_refs.locator: 2 Applications to Learning, Repeated Games, State Dependent Noise, and Queue Optimization p. 29
source_refs.source_title: Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The heteroscedastic sub-Gaussian regime requires \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0\) and, for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), \[\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda\varepsilon_t)\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2\sigma^2(x_t)}{2}\right)\quad\text{almost surely}.\] When conditional variances exist, this implies \(\operatorname{Var}(y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t)\le\sigma^2(x_t)\). A homoscedastic guarantee transfers directly only when it uses a valid uniform envelope \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\sigma(x)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heteroscedastic feedback has centered observation noise whose variance or tail scale changes with the queried input.
knowledge_statements.title: Heteroscedastic Noise

children.title: Heavy-Tailed Noise
children.top_down_role: Feedback regimes with weak tail control or limited moments.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[|\varepsilon_t|^{1+\alpha}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le V\) almost surely for some \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The direct tail consequence of bounded low-order conditional moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathbb E[|\varepsilon_t|^{1+\alpha}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le V\) for \(\alpha>0\), then for every \(u>0\), \[\Pr(|\varepsilon_t|>u\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t)\le\frac{V}{u^{1+\alpha}}\quad\text{almost surely}.\] This polynomial bound is the universal tail control supplied by the moment assumption; exponential decay does not follow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded low-order moment yields polynomial tail control by Markov's inequality, not sub-Gaussian exponential decay.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Tail Bound from a Finite Moment
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Tail Bound from a Finite Moment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Centered Pareto Noise Is Not Sub-Gaussian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-low-order-moment heavy-tail counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) satisfy \(\Pr(Z>u)=u^{-\beta}\) for \(u\ge1\), where \(1<\beta<2\), and let \(\varepsilon=SZ\) for an independent Rademacher sign \(S\). Then \(\mathbb E\varepsilon=0\), \(\mathbb E|\varepsilon|^p<\infty\) exactly when \(p<\beta\), \(\mathbb E\varepsilon^2=\infty\), and \(\mathbb E e^{\lambda\varepsilon}=\infty\) for every \(\lambda\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric Pareto noise is centered and has low-order moments but infinite variance and no finite nonzero MGF.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is independent of \(Z\) and is uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Centered Pareto Noise Is Not Sub-Gaussian

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional subclass with polynomially decaying tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonnegative random variable \(Z\) has a regularly varying tail of index \(\beta>0\) if \[\Pr(Z>u)=u^{-\beta}L(u),\qquad u\to\infty,\] where \(L(cu)/L(u)\to1\) for every \(c>0\). Then \(\mathbb E[Z^p]<\infty\) for \(p<\beta\) and \(\mathbb E[Z^p]=\infty\) for \(p>\beta\); the boundary \(p=\beta\) depends on \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular variation formalizes polynomial heavy tails and determines moment existence away from the boundary order.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is positive and slowly varying at infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularly Varying Heavy-Tail Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive heavy-tailed feedback specified directly by a uniform conditional tail envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For predictable queries \(x_t\), centered errors \(\varepsilon_t\) belong to \(\mathsf{PT}(\beta,A,u_0)\) if \[\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0,\qquad \Pr(|\varepsilon_t|>u\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t)\le Au^{-\beta}\] almost surely for every \(t\) and \(u\ge u_0\). This condition is uniform over adaptively selected queries but does not require independence across rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional polynomial-tail class imposes a uniform power-law tail envelope on adaptively queried, conditionally centered errors without requiring temporal independence.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable.
The errors are conditionally integrable and centered.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Polynomial-Tail Feedback Class

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nesting of Uniform Conditional Moment Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of adaptive heavy-tail moment assumptions with respect to moment order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(0<p<q\) and \(\mathbb E[|\varepsilon_t|^q\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le V_q\) almost surely, uniformly in \(t\). Then \[\mathbb E[|\varepsilon_t|^p\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le V_q^{p/q}\quad\text{almost surely}.\] The converse fails in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform higher conditional moment bound implies every lower conditional moment bound, but lower moments need not imply higher ones.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[|\varepsilon_t|^q\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le V_q<\infty\) almost surely for every round.

notation.meaning: lower and higher conditional moment orders

knowledge_statements.title: Nesting of Uniform Conditional Moment Classes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-moment heavy-tailed feedback regime for predictable sequential queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_t\) be \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable and write \(y_t=f(x_t)+\varepsilon_t\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) and \(V<\infty\), the errors form a conditionally centered \((1+\alpha)\)-moment-bounded class when, almost surely for every \(t\), \[\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0,\qquad \mathbb E[|\varepsilon_t|^{1+\alpha}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le V.\] The condition allows dependence through the history and does not imply conditional independence or a sub-Gaussian moment-generating-function bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-tailed adaptive feedback may be defined by predictable queries, conditional centering, and a uniform low-order conditional moment bound; temporal independence and sub-Gaussian tails are not implied.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t\) is predictable with respect to \((\mathcal F_t)\).
The displayed conditional expectations exist.
\(\alpha\in(0,1]\) and \(V<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon_t\text{ belongs to a uniform adaptive conditional }(1+\alpha)\text{-moment class}.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Conditional Moment-Bounded Noise Class

assumptions_latex: Observations satisfy \(y_t=f(x_t)+\varepsilon_t\) with conditionally centered errors.
For some \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) and \(V<\infty\), a conditional \((1+\alpha)\)-moment is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-moment control alone does not imply a sub-Gaussian moment-generating-function bound, so sub-Gaussian confidence guarantees do not apply unchanged.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bounded low-order conditional moments are a canonical heavy-tailed feedback model
authoritative robust-bandit or robust-Bayesian-optimization source needed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment-bounded heavy-tailed noise, allowing infinite variance when \(\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A moment-bounded heavy-tailed regime is specified by \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0\) and constants \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), \(V<\infty\) such that \[\mathbb E[|\varepsilon_t|^{1+\alpha}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\le V\quad\text{almost surely}.\] This condition permits infinite variance when \(\alpha<1\) and does not supply a finite sub-Gaussian moment-generating function. Therefore guarantees derived from empirical-mean Gaussian or sub-Gaussian concentration require additional truncation, clipping, median-of-means estimation, or another robust feedback construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-tailed noise may have only a bounded low-order moment, invalidating ordinary sub-Gaussian confidence bounds and requiring robust estimation.
knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tailed Noise

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The moment-bounded heavy-tail condition and failure of automatic sub-Gaussian concentration are mathematically sound, but no authoritative robust-bandit or robust-optimization source is supplied.

assumptions_latex: The observations are independent.
They share mean \(\mu\) and each has variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
\(1\le k\le n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust mean estimation at the finite-variance boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) be independent with common mean \(\mu\) and variance at most \(\sigma^2\). Partition them into k equal retained blocks of size \(m=\lfloor n/k\rfloor\), and take the median of the block means. Under a compatible median convention, \[\Pr\!\left(|\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{MOM}}-\mu|>\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt m}\right)\le e^{-k/8}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Median-of-means can restore high-probability mean confidence under independent finite-variance observations, but this algorithm belongs to the robust-feedback leaf.
knowledge_statements.title: Median-of-Means Confidence Under Finite Variance
